title: Locked in: How formal institutional design sustains extractivism and ecological decline in Ghana’s mining–water sector
summary: Mining-related water pollution persists despite repeated legislative reforms and regulatory interventions. Yet, existing explanations largely attribute this persistence to weak enforcement, political patronage, or socioeconomic pressures driving artisanal small-scale mining (ASM). We argue instead that the problem is fundamentally one of institutional design. Drawing on institutional theory and institutional grammar analysis, we examine how Ghana's mining-water legislation allocates authority and embeds incentive structures that shape environmental governance. We find that the legislative framework privileges regulative over constitutive institutional elements, producing governance arrangements that are procedurally elaborate yet functionally weak. At the same time, it embeds economic and political incentives that favor extractivism while providing comparatively weak social and regulatory incentives for environmental stewardship, reinforcing fragmented authority, symbolic governance, and executive overreach. These institutional arrangements generate intertwined common-pool resource and public-bad dilemmas that lock Ghana's mining-water sector into a gilded trap, in which short-term extractive gains systematically outweigh long-term socioecological sustainability. The findings suggest that persistent mining-related water pollution is not simply a failure of enforcement but a consequence of institutional architectures that privilege extractivism while weakening environmental governance. In reconceptualizing the gilded trap as an institutionally produced condition, the paper demonstrates how imbalances between constitutive and regulative institutional elements generate symbolic governance and position the state as an active producer, rather than merely a failed regulator, of extractivist outcomes.

summary: The article econometrically assesses the impact of human capital on the development of Uzbekistan's digital economy under the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, using data for 2010-2024. A three-component composite digital economy index (DEI) is constructed, and human capital is proxied by tertiary enrolment. Autoregressive distributed lag (ADL) models are estimated with Newey-West (HAC) standard errors, including a regime dummy and an interaction term for the AI policy period. Policy proposals for enriching human capital with AI competencies are developed.

title: DIGITAL FINANCIAL INCLUSION AND ITS IMPACT ON RURAL ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT IN INDIA: OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES
summary: Digital financial access is now a major focus in India’s economic plans. In many places, it has reshaped how rural households save, pay for daily costs, and put money aside for the future. This work reviews what happened as digital finance spread in rural areas. It looks at clear outcomes and the spillover effects on local trade and jobs. It further studies how these changes relate to household risk and to the day-to-day work of small firms, including whether they can expand. Over the past decade, public programs and private services reduced barriers to banking. Efforts tied to JAM, along with wider links to Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, and mobile service, helped widen coverage. At the same time, fintech companies offered new payment methods and easier ways to use accounts. Now, a large share of rural residents who earlier had no bank account can use formal accounts. Many can send and receive digital payments with little delay. Benefit money can also arrive faster. In some cases, small loans that used to be hard to obtain are now within reach. However, rapid digital adoption has also highlighted serious problems: a gender device gap, uneven digital literacy, weak rural infrastructure, and rising cyber scams. Utilizing recent data from government bodies, the Reserve Bank of India, and major development organizations, this paper examines how digital finance alters behaviour in rural settings before and after digitization. It checks changes before and after digitization. It focuses on whether income stays steadier, whether people can get credit more easily, and how farmers connect to markets. The results point to a clear pattern. Access to digital services can help reduce poverty. Still, access by itself is not enough. Lasting economic gains need more than better apps. Policy should also include clear financial know how for users, stronger rules against misuse, and better ground level infrastructure.

summary: Digital transformation in micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) is no longer limited to technology adoption but encompasses organizational readiness, technology integration, business model transformation, and sustainability within digital ecosystems. This study contributes by integrating these dimensions into a more comprehensive understanding of how MSMEs develop and sustain digital transformation within interconnected business environments. title: DIGITAL CAPABILITY, WORK REDESIGN, AND EFFICIENCY: A STUDY OF INDIAN MANUFACTURING FIRMS
summary: Digital transformation is often described as a path to manufacturing efficiencies with the introduction of connected equipment, enterprise software and manufacturing data but fails to conceal that this is where the efficiencies are going. In this paper, we look at the management issue of making digital investments into the appropriate employee behaviours and integrated organizational processes. Suggests a combined effect of employee digital capability and work redesign is necessary to conclude whether the digital transformation can lead to increased efficiency in Indian manufacturing firm. Based on Indian empirical research, official data and work design theory, the paper proposes a capability–redesign–efficiency matrix and evaluates the extent of the evidence. Covered industries grew by 11.89% in gross value added (GVA) current prices in 2022–23 to 2023–24 and by 5.92% in employment. Additionally, the percentage of unincorporated non-agricultural establishments that used the internet increased from 26.7 per cent in 2023–24 to 39.4 per cent in 2025. Even if neither can be used to prove that digital transformation is an efficiency gain, combining both highlights the need for considering the evolution in production capacity alongside variable levels of digital uptake. Digital capability has more value when employees see and make sense of information, act on exceptions, and improve the process; work redesign provides them the decision rights, coordination procedures, and backstops to make them productive. Evaluation of the multilevel research design is designed for further testing with employees' responses and with observed plant results. The suggested gift is a more accurate description of how digital transformation can improve employee and/or organizational efficiency and when it cannot.

title: The Role Of International Environmental Conventions In Shaping Domestic Environmental Law: A Critical Analysis With Special Reference To India
summary: Environmental problems have never fitted neatly within political boundaries. Pollution can cross borders through air and water, hazardous waste can be transported from one country to another, and greenhouse gas emissions affect the global climate irrespective of where they originate. International environmental conventions have consequently become an important part of environmental governance. Their influence, however, does not end with international negotiations. The more interesting legal question is what happens when these commitments enter domestic legal systems. This article examines how international environmental conventions have shaped Indian environmental law, with particular attention to the Stockholm Conference of 1972, the Rio Declaration of 1992, major environmental conventions and protocols, and the development of Indian environmental legislation and judicial principles. It argues that the influence of international environmental law in India has operated through three principal routes: legislative implementation, constitutional interpretation and judicial development of environmental principles. At the same time, international commitments do not automatically become enforceable domestic law. The gap between international promises and domestic implementation remains a significant limitation. The Indian experience therefore shows that the real legal impact of an environmental convention is determined not simply by ratification, but by what the State subsequently does with the obligation.

title: Trade, Competition And Market Access In The European Union: Assessing The Effectiveness Of EU Competition Law In Preserving Fair And Open Markets
summary: The EU Internal Market is a zone of free circulation of goods, services, capital, and people. At the same time, for the free circulation to be realized, it is necessary to ensure legal and institutional guarantees. The influence of cartels (consortiums of companies on a particular commodity), anti-competitive government interventions, different national policies, and the predominant position of giant digital companies in the market also affect the free circulation of goods in the EU. The EU has a well-developed legal framework for ensuring competition in the internal market. This legislation regulates anti-competitive agreements (article 101), abuse of dominance (article 102), and state aid (article 107). Recently, EU legislation has been developing digital-specific regulations, such as the DMA and DSA, to ensure the competitiveness of the EU internal market in the digital economy. EU competition law appears to be one of the most effective ways to ensure openness and competitiveness in the EU. In addition, it should be noted that such competition laws enable not only to ensure the free circulation of goods in the EU but also to enhance the competitiveness of enterprises. For instance, the EU should consolidate its tools for regulating entry barriers and separation of competition policy from economic policy to enhance the free circulation of goods within EU member states. Moreover, to ensure the free circulation of goods in the EU, it would be useful to develop competition policy oversight authorities to ensure and enforce regulations in the digital economy.

title: Tax Evasion, Corporate Governance, and ESG Disclosure: A Systematic Literature Review of Emerging Patterns and Research Frontiers (2000–2025)
summary: This study presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of 95 peer-reviewed international and national journal articles published between 2020 and 2025, examining the interrelationships among tax morale, agency problems, institutional quality, sustainability pressure, and ESG disclosure in the context of corporate tax evasion and avoidance. Following the PRISMA protocol, this review synthesizes evidence drawn from leading databases including Scopus, ScienceDirect, Emerald Insight, and Taylor & Francis Online, as well as top-ranked Indonesian journals indexed in Sinta 1 and Sinta 2. The findings consistently demonstrate that elevated tax morale, anchored in ethical consciousness and robust social norms, substantially curtails opportunistic tax behavior and strengthens compliance among both individual taxpayers and corporate entities. Nonetheless, agency conflicts remain a structural challenge: information asymmetries between managers and stakeholders frequently precipitate reduced transparency, earnings manipulation, and aggressive tax avoidance strategies—particularly in institutional environments characterized by weak regulatory enforcement. Conversely, high-quality institutional frameworks—marked by sound governance mechanisms, credible regulatory bodies, and effective rule of law significantly mitigate agency costs and enhance the reliability of ESG disclosures. The review also reveals a growing convergence between sustainability mandates and tax governance: as regulators, investors, and civil society intensify pressure for responsible corporate behavior, firms increasingly improve the scope and credibility of their ESG reporting, which in turn constrains tax aggressiveness. This review contributes to the literature by mapping the theoretical evolution of tax research, identifying persistent methodological gaps, and proposing an integrative agenda that aligns tax policy, corporate governance, and sustainable development. Implications for policymakers and practitioners especially in developing economies such as Indonesia are discussed in detail. title: AI and cloud adoption in European banking: Country-level evidence on the profitability-cyber risk trade-off
summary: This study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, banking profitability, and ICT-related cyber risk across 28 European countries. These countries are selected because of persistent profitability pressures in the banking sector, rising digital transformation costs, and increasing exposure to cyber threats within a context of uneven digital maturity and cyber resilience. Using a recent cross-sectional dataset covering the EU-27 and Norway, we investigate the risk–return implications of AI adoption. Cloud computing is considered both as a key digital infrastructure and as a moderating factor in the relationship between AI adoption, return on equity (ROE), and cyber risk. Methodologically, the study employs a cross-sectional quantitative design combining Hierarchical Cluster Analysis and Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA) to address heterogeneity and model uncertainty. These issues are particularly relevant given substantial differences across countries in digital maturity, institutional capacity, and risk exposure. The empirical analysis is conducted using R version 4.2.2. Our results reveal a strong association between AI adoption and cloud computing. AI adoption is negatively associated with ROE, suggesting that implementation costs, organizational adjustment, and learning frictions may precede profitability gains. In contrast, cloud computing is positively associated with ICT-related cyber risk and strengthens the positive relationship between AI adoption and cyber risk, highlighting a trade-off between digital capability and operational vulnerability. Overall, the study contributes to the AI–finance literature by integrating profitability and cyber-risk perspectives within a digital complementarity framework. The results indicate that the outcomes of AI adoption depend on digital infrastructure, institutional readiness, and cyber resilience, with implications for balanced digital transformation and financial stability.

title: Digital Transformation in Retail Banking: Fintech's Effect on Service Quality and Customer Satisfaction in Mumbai
summary: Abstract: Introduction The rapid diffusion of financial technology (fintech) has fundamentally reshaped the delivery of retail banking services across urban India, with Mumbai the country's financial capital serving as an early adopter of digital banking innovation. Mobile banking applications, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), robo-advisory tools, artificial-intelligence-driven chatbots and contactless payment systems have altered the manner in which customers interact with banks, raising important questions about how these technologies shape perceived service quality and, in turn, customer satisfaction. Purpose This study examines the extent to which fintech adoption influences the five SERVQUAL dimensions of service quality reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy and tangibles and overall customer satisfaction among retail banking customers in Mumbai. Methodology A descriptive and analytical research design was adopted. Primary data were collected from a sample of 100 retail banking customers in Mumbai through a structured questionnaire administered on a five-point Likert scale, supplemented by secondary data drawn from journals, RBI publications, NPCI reports and bank disclosures. Percentage analysis, mean analysis and Karl Pearson's correlation analysis were used to examine the relationships in the data. Findings Fintech adoption was found to be positively associated with customer-perceived service quality and satisfaction, with responsiveness and convenience-related dimensions showing the strongest association among Mumbai's retail banking customers. Respondents in the 21–40 age group and those with higher digital literacy reported significantly greater satisfaction with fintech-enabled banking channels than with traditional branch banking. All three hypotheses were statistically confirmed: a one-sample t-test showed fintech adoption is significantly related to perceived service quality (t = 12.46, p = 0.000); Karl Pearson's correlation confirmed a strong positive relationship between fintech-driven service quality and customer satisfaction (r = 0.72, p = 0.000); and a one-way ANOVA confirmed that satisfaction differs significantly across age groups (F = 3.85, p = 0.012). Implications The findings carry implications for retail banks seeking to refine digital-channel strategy, for regulators concerned with consumer protection and digital financial inclusion, and for future researchers seeking to extend the service-quality literature into the fintech domain.

title: CSR in Indian Companies: From Philanthropy to Legal Mandate
summary: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) in India has changed considerably from the traditional model of corporate charity and the Gandhian trusteeship model. It is now a mandatory, strategic business framework that builds environmental and social benefits into core operations. Rooted in India’s long heritage of business responsibility, CSR underwent a significant transition after the economic liberalization of the 1990s, moving from philanthropy-based methods to a multi-stakeholder model that addresses financial stakeholders, workers and communities. CSR became a formal accountability mechanism on 1 April 2014, when Section 135 of the landmark Companies Act, 2013 came into force, requiring qualifying companies to spend at least 2% of their average net profits on CSR initiatives. Today, CSR goes beyond philanthropic contributions to serve as a crucial strategic instrument that promotes ethical behavior and sustainable environmental practices while aligning company operations with societal expectations. This paper analyzes the current landscape of CSR in India, tracing its development from conventional philanthropy to a mandatory strategic business model, and examines present practices, implementation hurdles and future possibilities. It investigates the regulatory framework governing CSR, including the Companies Act, 2013, the attendant compliance obligations and the mechanisms for enforcement. The paper seeks to contribute to the academic discourse on CSR in India and to inform policymakers, businesses, academia and civil society about the opportunities and challenges in fostering corporate sustainability and social welfare.

title: Financial Reporting Completeness and the Quality of Audit Reports: Evidence from Kenyan Public Universities
summary: Financial reporting completeness is critical to the credibility of financial information and the effectiveness of external auditing in public institutions. In Kenyan public universities, weaknesses in the completeness of financial statements, disclosures, supporting documentation, and reporting of financial obligations may affect audit report quality. This study evaluated the influence of financial reporting completeness on audit report quality in Kenyan public universities. The study was guided by Agency Theory and adopted a positivist research philosophy and cross-sectional research design. The target population comprised 175 respondents drawn from 35 publicly chartered universities in Kenya, including Deputy Vice Chancellors (Finance and Administration), Chief Finance Officers, internal auditors, accountants, and members of audit or finance committees. The study used a census approach at the institutional level, while purposive sampling selected respondents with direct knowledge of financial reporting and audit processes. The study collected primary data using structured questionnaires and obtained secondary data from published financial statements and audit reports. A pilot study involving 40 respondents from four public chartered universities achieved a 100% response rate. Reliability analysis established Cronbach?s alpha coefficients of 0.886 for financial reporting completeness and 0.914 for audit report quality, confirming satisfactory internal consistency. Data from 151 respondents, representing an 86.3% response rate, were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and simple linear regression. Descriptive findings indicated that financial reporting completeness was practiced to a moderately high extent (M = 3.68, SD = 1.16). Pearson correlation analysis found a strong, positive, and statistically significant relationship between financial reporting completeness and audit report quality (r = .711, p < .001). Regression analysis further showed that financial reporting completeness significantly predicted audit report quality, explaining 50.6% of its variation (R? = .506, adjusted R? = .503). The regression model was statistically significant, F (1,149) = 152.33, p < .001, while financial reporting completeness had a positive and statistically significant effect on audit report quality (B = .295, ? = .711, t = 12.366, p < .001). The null hypothesis was therefore rejected. The study concludes that greater completeness of financial reporting is associated with higher-quality audit reports. Public universities should strengthen financial reporting completeness, particularly in disclosing contingent liabilities, potential financial obligations, and future financial risks, alongside stronger pre-audit financial reporting reviews.

title: Underground Coal Mine Fires in Dhanbad, Jharkhand: A Need for Comprehensive State Legislation to Protect the Right to Life and Environment
summary: The underground coal mine fires in the Jharia Coalfield of Dhanbad, Jharkhand, constitute one of India’s longest-running environmental and humanitarian crises. Burning continuously for over a century, these fires have caused extensive environmental degradation, air pollution, land subsidence, destruction of valuable coal reserves, and widespread displacement of local communities. Continuous exposure to toxic gases and particulate matter has resulted in serious public health concerns, including respiratory diseases, cardiovascular disorders, and other chronic illnesses, thereby threatening the fundamental right to life and a healthy environment guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. Although several central enactments, including the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, and the Mines Act, 1952, provide a general framework for environmental protection and mining regulation, they do not adequately address the unique challenges posed by underground coal mine fires. This article critically examines the constitutional and statutory obligations of the Union and the State Governments in preventing mine fires, protecting public health, ensuring environmental restoration, and rehabilitating affected communities. It argues that the absence of a comprehensive state-specific legal framework has contributed to fragmented governance and ineffective implementation of existing policies. The article proposes the enactment of a dedicated Jharkhand Underground Coal Mine Fire Prevention, Rehabilitation and Environmental Protection Act, establishing an independent statutory authority for fire prevention, environmental monitoring, scientific risk assessment, rehabilitation, compensation, and inter-agency coordination. Adopting a doctrinal research methodology based on constitutional provisions, statutory analysis, judicial precedents, government reports, and secondary literature, the article concludes that comprehensive state legislation is essential to uphold environmental justice, strengthen environmental governance, protect public health, ensure accountable rehabilitation, and secure the rights of present and future generations.

title: Reform of the state-owned enterprise wage determination system and pay gap
summary: Purpose Excessive income inequality is a significant obstacle to achieving shared prosperity in China. Using Chinese listed firms from 2016 to 2021, we test the effect of the reform of the state-owned enterprise wage determination system on the pay gap between executives and ordinary employees. Design/methodology/approach Based on data from Chinese A-share listed companies from 2016 to 2021, we employ the difference-in-differences model to study the impact of state-owned enterprise wage system reform on the pay gap between executives and ordinary employees. Findings We find that the reform narrows the pay gap between executives and ordinary employees. This conclusion holds after a series of robustness tests. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the effect of the reform on the pay gap is more pronounced for firms in regions with lower income disparity and firms with weaker corporate governance. Mechanism tests indicate that the reform reduces the pay gap by reducing executive compensation rather than affecting ordinary employees' wages. Originality/value This paper provides new evidence on the role of the reform in firms and offers important policy implications for other countries.

title: Mechanisms for ensuring the digital transformation of industrial enterprises
summary: The article examines the aspects of the digital transformation of industrial enterprises amid technological, economic, and institutional change. The study is relevant because digital transformation has moved beyond implementing individual information systems and technological solutions to encompass changes in business processes, organizational approaches, management systems, resource utilization, and mechanisms for creating economic value. For Ukrainian industrial enterprises, this issue has become particularly urgent because they must simultaneously restore production capacity, modernize technology, maintain operational resilience, and adapt to the new requirements of the digital economy. The study aims to analyze and systematize the theoretical and methodological framework for developing mechanisms for industrial enterprises’ digital transformation. To achieve this purpose, the article clarifies the concepts of “digitization,” “digitalization,” and “digital transformation.” It establishes that the digital transformation of an industrial enterprise should be viewed as a systemic process of restructuring technological, production, managerial, organizational, and market relationships through the integration of digital technologies, data, and digital competencies. Unlike fragmented automation of individual operations, digital transformation involves extending technological changes across interconnected business processes, the management system, and value-creation mechanisms. The conditions for digital transformation in industrial enterprises fall into four main groups: technological, organizational, resource-related, and institutional. Technological conditions include digital infrastructure, the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence, robotics, big data, and digital twins; organizational and intangible conditions include digital culture, competencies, organizational flexibility, strategic orientation, managerial support, and data governance; resource-related conditions include financial, investment, human, information, and time resources; institutional conditions include public policy, financial support, the regulatory environment, the innovation ecosystem, and international integration. This study examines current trends in digital development in enterprises in the European Union and Ukraine and identifies differences in the adoption of basic and advanced digital technologies. For Ukrainian industrial enterprises, insufficient financial and human capacity to scale digital solutions remains a significant constraint, particularly amid wartime uncertainty and competition for resources between restoring production capacities and investing in digital solutions. The mechanism for ensuring digital transformation should be an integrated system of interconnected technological, organizational, financial, human-resource, informational, and institutional components. Align the digital strategy with the enterprise’s overall development strategy, secure adequate resources and financial support, develop employees’ digital competencies, integrate digital technologies into key business processes, and account for digital maturity, financial capacity, production-specific characteristics, and external environmental risks. Keywords: digital transformation, digitalization, industrial enterprises, financial support, digital investments, financial mechanisms, digital maturity.

title: The Substantive Impact of the UK "Say on Pay" Regime on Executive Compensation Levels
summary: This paper examines the substantive impact of the UK “say on pay” regime on executive compensation levels. It first outlines the regime’s legislative development, dual-track information disclosure system and two-tier shareholder voting mechanism consisting of binding votes on remuneration policies and advisory votes on implementation reports. The study finds that the regime has failed to curb the sustained growth of total executive compensation, yet it has promoted the shift of pay structure towards a performance-oriented model and expanded the application of long-term incentive plans, while strong shareholder opposition can drive targeted pay adjustments in individual cases. The paper further attributes the limited effectiveness to internal corporate governance flaws, the non-binding nature of most voting outcomes and structural problems in shareholding. Finally, it puts forward targeted reform proposals, concluding that further institutional improvements are required to better align executive pay with corporate performance.

title: Financial instruments for ensuring the digital development of industrial enterprises
summary: This article identifies promising financial instruments to support the digital transformation of industrial enterprises in Ukraine. It reviews global experience regarding financial tools for digitalization. The study identifies the key benefits of digitalizing Ukraine’s industrial sector: increased production productivity, cost reduction, enhanced product competitiveness and export potential, optimized resource utilization, greater resilience of industrial enterprises amidst wartime and economic challenges, integration into international production and logistics chains, and the creation of prerequisites for innovation-driven growth and technological modernization based on sustainability principles. The article outlines specific factors determining the choice and complementary application of financial instruments for the digital development of Ukrainian industrial enterprises. These include high capital intensity and production complexity, the high cost of technological upgrades, significant diversity among industrial enterprises, the strong export orientation of Ukrainian industry, extensive damage and destruction caused by the military conflict, and limited internal financial capacity and access to long-term financial resources. The analysis examined the funding sources for capital investments by Ukrainian industrial enterprises. The analysis found that equity-based financing currently serves as the primary instrument for supporting digital processes. The study substantiates key promising instruments for financing the digital transformation of industrial enterprises, categorized by their level of digital maturity. It is established that for the initial level of digital maturity, priority instruments include service models, operating leases, retained earnings, depreciation charges, concessional loan programs (such as the “5-7-9%” scheme), crowdfunding, and regranting; for the intermediate level—financial leases, syndicated loans, loan guarantees, mezzanine capital, risk insurance, and crowd-investing; and for the high level—corporate venture capital, green bonds, smart contracts, international grants, and asset tokenization. title: The Role of the Sagarmala Project in Helping Indian Businesses Achieve ESG Goals
summary: Introduction: The Sagarmala Project, an ambitious initiative by the Government of India, is designed to modernize port infrastructure, enhance logistics efficiency, and promote coastal economic development. As businesses increasingly align with Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) principles, this project provides a significant opportunity to support sustainability, social responsibility, and transparent governance. With over 7,500 km of coastline and vast inland waterways, India holds significant potential for maritime-led development, and the initiative plays a pivotal role in reducing logistics costs and increasing the competitiveness of Indian businesses in global trade. Methodology: The study uses a systematic literature review to compare road and maritime transport in terms of cost, emissions and efficiency. The theoretical framework is based on ESG principles to assess maritime sustainability. Model selection uses comparative models of road versus sea transport, evaluating cost per ton-km to assess economic feasibility, emission outputs to quantify environmental benefits, and operational efficiency metrics such as cargo capacity and fuel consumption rates. An ESG assessment framework is incorporated to measure the Sagarmala Project's impact on corporate sustainability, carbon reduction and supply chain resilience. A conceptual framework is developed to illustrate the relationship between transportation mode selection, carbon emissions and logistics costs, and ESG performance improvements through coastal and inland water transport. Results & Discussion: Maritime transport cuts emissions by up to 40% and costs by 30% compared to road transport (Rodrigue et al., 2020; World Bank, 2022), while Kumar and Patel (2021) estimate that port-led development under Sagarmala could cut India's carbon footprint by 33-35% by 2030. Coastal shipping consumes only 10% of the energy required for road transport, and a standard cargo ship can move one ton of goods approximately 500 km per litre of fuel against 50-100 km for a truck, making sea transport nearly 5-10 times more fuel-efficient. Ships can carry up to 200,000 tons of cargo compared with 20-40 tons per truck. India's road network spans 6.4 million km and manages 64.5% of freight; the project aims to shift 25-30% of road freight to maritime transport. Transitioning could reduce logistics costs by 30-50% while cutting CO₂ emissions by 80%, given that road transport accounts for 75% of transport-related CO₂ emissions against 11% from shipping. The project is expected to create over 10 million jobs and has mobilised over ₹5 lakh crore in investments, supported by a 40% discount on vessel and cargo charges and a GST reduction on bunker fuels from 18% to 5%. Conclusion: The Sagarmala Project presents a transformative opportunity for Indian businesses to embed Environmental, Social, and Governance principles into their operations. By enhancing logistical efficiency, reducing environmental impact, and promoting social inclusivity, it serves as a model for sustainable economic growth while aligning with India's global ESG commitments. Sea transport offers a significantly more fuel-efficient, cost-effective and environmentally friendly alternative compared to road transport, and with policy incentives, infrastructure development and increased private sector involvement, coastal shipping can revolutionize India's supply chain. To ensure long-term success, it is essential to address last-mile connectivity issues and streamline regulatory frameworks.

title: OFF-BUDGET FINANCING, CENTRAL BANK MANDATES, AND LONG-TERM INVESTMENT MOBILIZATION IN INDONESIA
summary: In recent years, the increasing emphasis on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) issues has transformed the way companies communicate their performance and long-term sustainability. This study aims to examine the impact of ESG disclosure and sustainability accounting practices on firm value in the context of Indonesian listed companies. By integrating the concept of transparency and stakeholder trust, this research explores whether more comprehensive ESG reporting contributes to enhanced market valuation and investor confidence. This study employs a quantitative research approach using secondary data collected from annual reports and sustainability reports of publicly listed companies in Indonesia. ESG disclosure is measured using a disclosure index based on widely recognized reporting standards, while sustainability accounting practices are proxied through the extent of environmental and social cost recognition. Firm value is measured using indicators such as Tobin’s Q and market-to-book ratio. The data are analyzed using multiple regression techniques to assess the relationship between variables. The findings are expected to demonstrate that higher levels of ESG disclosure and more robust sustainability accounting practices positively influence firm value. Companies that provide transparent and comprehensive ESG information are more likely to gain investor trust, reduce information asymmetry, and strengthen their reputation in the capital market. Furthermore, sustainability accounting practices are anticipated to reinforce the credibility of ESG disclosures by providing measurable and accountable financial information related to sustainability activities. This research contributes to the growing body of literature on sustainability reporting and corporate value, particularly in emerging markets like Indonesia. It also provides practical implications for corporate managers, regulators, and investors by highlighting the importance of integrating ESG considerations into financial reporting frameworks. Ultimately, this study underscores the role of transparency in building trust, which in turn enhances firm value and supports sustainable economic development.

title: Digital transformation as a driver of participation in global value chains
summary: The article examines how digital transformation deepens countries’ participation in global value chains. The study aims to substantiate the mechanisms through which digitalization influences countries’ integration into global production networks and to identify strategic directions for strengthening trade and digital development. The study uses systems analysis, comparison, generalization, and synthesis of international experience. The findings show that digital technologies reduce transaction costs, improve coordination efficiency, and facilitate cross-border trade procedures. The results indicate that digital infrastructure alone is insufficient to ensure deeper participation in GVCs, as its effects depend on complementarity with trade openness, trade facilitation, and investment linkages. Broadband and mobile infrastructure create the basis for digital inclusion, while trade openness strengthens integration into international production networks. At the same time, FDI does not automatically generate technology and knowledge spillovers, highlighting the importance of linkages between foreign investors and local SMEs. International experience demonstrates that Smart Customs and Single Window systems can reduce administrative and time costs in cross-border trade. Integrating these systems with artificial intelligence, distributed ledger technologies, and the Internet of Things expands opportunities for digital verification, customs control, cargo monitoring, and supply-chain transparency. These mechanisms can facilitate SME integration into GVCs by reducing barriers to international production networks. The study’s scientific novelty lies in developing an integrated approach that combines digital, trade, and investment mechanisms for GVC integration. The study’s practical significance is reflected in the proposed strategic directions for trade and digital policy. Further research should quantitatively assess the complementary effects of digital readiness and trade facilitation on countries’ participation in GVCs. title: Adaptive approaches to digital project management under hybrid work formats
summary: The study is relevant because management systems must adapt to dynamic changes in the digital environment, the growing role of distributed teams, the increasing dependence of business processes on digital interaction, and the need to maintain stable team coordination amid the transformation of organizational work models. The article examines adaptive approaches to digital project management under mixed work formats, analyzes international companies’ practices, and develops a concept for adaptive digital project management that accounts for the changing digital environment. In the research process, the study used comparative analysis, systematization, structural and logical analysis, graphic modeling, and analytical generalization of international companies’ management practices. The study identified the essence of adaptive management in coordinating digital projects and characterized how mixed work formats transform management mechanisms. The analysis examined the practices of international companies Microsoft, Atlassian, Spotify, GitLab, Canva, Notion, and SoftServe in flexible work organization, digital collaboration, asynchronous communication, dynamic leadership, human capital development, and support for team interaction. The study identified key factors in adaptive management effectiveness, including the organization’s digital maturity, the level of team autonomy, the quality of internal communication, and the ability to respond rapidly to changes in the external environment. The paper highlights common trends in adaptive management development, including the spread of digital process coordination, the development of team autonomy, support for innovation, continuous learning, and people-oriented management. The study developed the concept of adaptive management for digital projects, encompassing flexible work organization, digital collaboration, adaptive leadership, human capital development, an innovative organizational culture, and client-oriented management. The study also developed an algorithm for implementing adaptive management in digital projects, which gradually integrates organizational, technological, and managerial components into the process of coordinating team activities. The practical significance of the results lies in their potential to improve digital project management systems in organizations across various industries amid digital transformation and the widespread adoption of hybrid work models. title: Corporate Whistleblowing Channels and Regulatory Compliance in Multinational Enterprises
summary: Whistleblowing channels are significant tools used to enhance transparency, accountability, and ethical practices within multinational companies. With exposure to different laws and regulations as well as varying environments within different countries, it becomes a challenge for firms to remain compliant with all these requirements. The current research aims at exploring the use of whistleblowing channels as a strategy of enhancing compliance with various regulations and avoiding any kind of unethical conduct by multinational companies. Specifically, this research will explore the role of internal and external whistleblowing channels, anonymous whistleblowing channels, whistleblower protection, as well as corporate policies aimed at encouraging employees to blow the whistle. This is conceptual research that focuses on reviewing literature related to corporate governance and regulatory compliance. It will become evident that whistleblowing channels play a significant role in uncovering cases of fraud, corruption, financial irregularities, and other forms of unethical behavior in multinational companies. Furthermore, this research identifies some of the key challenges such as fear of retaliation, lack of trust among employees, cultural differences, issues with privacy of information, as well as legal differences in whistleblower protection laws within different countries. To conclude, the adoption of the whistleblowing process within the framework of compliance policy systems results in ethical decision-making and organizational sustainability.

title: The Effect of Accounting Understanding, Accounting System Utilization, Internal Audit, and Internal Control System on The Quality of Hospital Financial Statements: A Study at PT XYZ
summary: This study investigates the impact of accounting comprehension, the accounting systems utilization, internal audit, and internal control systems on the quality of financial statements at PT XYZ, a state-owned enterprise managing four hospitals and five clinics in East Java. A quantitative research design with an associative approach was employed, with purposive sampling to select respondents. The final samples comprised 35 respondents consisting of accounting and finance staff directly involved in preparing financial statements. Data were collected using questionnaires and analyzed through multiple linear regression. The findings simultaneously indicate that the four independent variables significantly affect the quality of financial statements, with a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.845. Thus, 84.5% of the variation in financial statement quality can be explained by the research model. Partially, accounting comprehension and the accounting systems utilization exert positive but insignificant effects. While internal audit and internal control systems have positive and significant effects, with internal control systems being the most dominant variable. These results underscore that the reliability of hospital financial reporting is more strongly determined by the effectiveness of organizational control and oversight mechanisms than by individual competence alone. This research is perceived to serve as an evaluation material for PT XYZ’s management in strengthening internal control systems and internal audit functions to improve the quality of financial statements sustainably.

title: CAN DIGITALIZATION REDUCE UNEMPLOYMENT IN EMERGING MUSLIM ECONOMIES? CONDITIONAL EVIDENCE
summary: This study examines whether digitalization contributes to reducing unemployment in emerging Muslim economies and explores the conditional roles of financial development, human capital, and economic uncertainty. Despite the rapid expansion of internet access and digital technologies, evidence on their employment effects remains inconclusive, particularly in developing and Muslim-majority countries. Using panel data from 14 emerging Muslim economies over the period 2005–2024, this study employs a Random Effects model to estimate both the direct and moderating effects of digitalization on unemployment. Internet penetration is used as a proxy for digitalization, while domestic credit to the private sector, human capital, and inflation volatility represent financial development, human capital, and economic uncertainty, respectively. The findings indicate that digitalization does not have a significant direct effect on unemployment. However, financial development significantly reduces unemployment, while human capital exhibits a positive direct relationship with unemployment, suggesting the presence of labor-market mismatches. Furthermore, the interaction analysis reveals that human capital and economic uncertainty significantly strengthen the unemployment-reducing effect of digitalization, whereas financial development does not play a significant moderating role. These results suggest that digital transformation alone is insufficient to improve labor-market outcomes and that supportive structural conditions are necessary to realize its employment benefits. The study contributes to the growing literature by providing new evidence from emerging Muslim economies and highlighting the importance of complementary factors in shaping the digitalization–unemployment nexus.

title: Optimalisasi Investasi Wakaf Uang melalui Diversifikasi Aset dan Peningkatan Kapasitas Nazhir: Studi Kasus Badan Wakaf Uang Muhammadiyah Sumatera Barat
summary: Aims: This study aims to analyze the optimization of waqf investment at Badan Wakaf Uang Muhammadiyah (BWUM) West Sumatra by focusing on waqf asset diversification, investment management, risk control, and the utilization of investment returns for community welfare. Method: This research employs a qualitative approach using an ex-post facto method. Data were collected through interviews and documentation related to waqf investment management at BWUM West Sumatra. The data were analyzed descriptively to examine the practices of investment development, supervision, reporting, risk management, and distribution of waqf benefits. Results: The findings indicate that BWUM West Sumatra has developed waqf funds through Islamic financial institutions and productive business activities, including UD Berkah. However, several investments have been discontinued due to considerations of efficiency and sustainability. Waqf investment management is supported by supervision, financial reporting, reserve fund establishment, and the distribution of investment benefits to social, educational, and healthcare sectors. These findings demonstrate that waqf investment optimization requires a balance between asset development, risk control, professional nazhir management, transparency, and the orientation toward public welfare. Conclusion/Novelty/Implications: The novelty of this study lies in its integrated analysis of waqf investment optimization by linking asset diversification, investment management, risk control, and the utilization of investment returns within the context of BWUM West Sumatra. The findings imply that strengthening nazhir professionalism, investment governance, transparency, and risk management is essential to ensure the sustainability and productivity of waqf assets. Future efforts should emphasize broader asset diversification, more strategic investment planning, and the development of productive waqf models that generate sustainable socio-economic benefits for the community.

title: Adaptive management of the strategic development of state-owned enterprises under conditions of uncertainty and non-systemic risks
summary: The article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations of adaptive management regarding the strategic development of state-owned enterprises amidst uncertainty and the impact of non-systemic risks. It argues for transforming the traditional approach to strategic management and shifting toward an adaptive model that enables timely responses to environmental changes. The article clarifies the essence of adaptive management for the strategic development of a state-owned enterprise, defining it as a continuous process that involves monitoring changes, identifying and assessing risks, determining the enterprise’s adaptive capacity, formulating alternative development scenarios, and adjusting strategic management decisions. The study distinguishes between systemic and non-systemic risks and categorizes non-systemic risks as operational, security-related, logistical, financial, personnel-related, technological, managerial, corporate, and reputational. The study identifies the components of a state-owned enterprise’s adaptive capacity, including strategic, organizational, financial, personnel, technological, operational, and risk-related adaptability. This study proposes a matrix-based approach to selecting a development strategy for a state-owned enterprise, grounded in comparing non-systemic risk levels with the enterprise’s adaptive capacity. Based on these factors, the study distinguishes four strategy types: preventive (low risk and low adaptive capacity), stabilization (high risk and low adaptive capacity), adaptive (high risk and high adaptive capacity), and transformational (low risk and high adaptive capacity). The practical significance of the proposed approach lies in its potential to support strategic decisions by state-owned enterprises by considering their risk exposure and their capacity to respond to changes in the external environment. Keywords: adaptive management, strategic development of enterprises, state-owned enterprises, non-systemic risks, uncertainty, adaptability, strategic decisions, development strategy, corporate governance, management of state-owned property.

title: Theorizing Cross‐Boundary Strategizing as Situated in Multilayered Supply Chains: A Strategy‐as‐Practice Approach to Supply Chain Management
summary: ABSTRACT Supply chain strategy is increasingly recognized as a multilayered phenomenon, with firms strategizing not only within their own boundaries but across supply chain tiers, jurisdictions, and wider regulatory and ecological systems. Yet most existing supply chain management research tends to treat these tiers, jurisdictions, and systems as contexts for strategizing rather than as something strategizing helps to constitute, leaving the cross‐boundary character undertheorized. This article introduces the strategy‐as‐practice (SAP) lens as an epistemic tool for theorizing cross‐boundary strategizing in multilayered supply chains. Drawing on SAP's tripartite framework of practices, practitioners, and praxis (three Ps), we show that strategizing is inherently cross‐boundary, both implicitly through the knowledge practitioners draw on beyond their organization and explicitly through direct interaction with counterparts in other firms and institutions. We introduce three approaches SAP scholars use to conceptualize the complex systems within which strategizing is situated: a “tall” ontology separating intraorganizational from extraorganizational practice, a “flat” ontology treating strategizing as a web of practices stretching sideways, and a zoom‐in/zoom‐out approach tracing connectivity and identifying consequentiality across layers. Using a heuristic case of a European solar company and its Chinese supplier network, we show how each approach can shape the research orientation and theoretical payoff. We close with a research agenda for cross‐boundary strategizing in supply chains and argue that supply chains have the potential to extend SAP's own theoretical apparatus.

summary: The rapid growth of social media and digital technologies has fundamentally altered the structure of mass media, shifting the audience's role from passive information recipients to active participants who create, disseminate, and shape media discourse. Drawing on theories of network society, the active audience, and media convergence, this article analyzes the key characteristics of social media audiences in the context of digital transformation and identifies the primary trends shaping this demographic in Vietnam. The study employs document analysis and synthesis, combined with a comparison of data from 2025 across popular social media platforms such as Facebook, YouTube, TikTok, Zalo, and Instagram. The findings reveal that contemporary media audiences are characterized by proactivity in content consumption and production, multidimensional interactivity, high fragmentation, network-based connectivity, and an increasingly significant influence on the formation of public opinion. Furthermore, four prominent trends are identified: the dominance of content distribution algorithms, the increasing personalization of media experiences, the emergence of closed information communities, and the expanding influence of audience groups capable of shaping public opinion. Based on these insights, the article proposes implications for media governance, journalism practices, and policymaking to adapt to the evolving nature of audiences in the digital media landscape.

title: When public money speaks: local government special bonds and corporate green innovation in China
summary: Public investment reallocates both resources and expectations. This study examines this dual role through China’s local government special bonds, a project-based fiscal instrument that reveals local governments’ green development priorities through observable and spatially targeted spending commitments. We construct a novel dataset of 146,601 special bond projects from 2019 to 2024, identify county-level allocations to the new-energy sector, and match them with Chinese A-share listed firms. We find that new-energy special bond allocation significantly increases corporate green innovation. The result is robust to alternative measures, Tobit estimation, winsorization, placebo tests using non-green patents, dynamic DID analysis, Bartik instrumental variables, propensity score matching, and entropy balancing. Mechanism tests show that corporate climate risk attention, measured from annual reports, partially mediates the effect, suggesting that targeted public investment guides managerial attention in addition to supplying capital. The effect is stronger where policy signals are more credible or easier to absorb, including regions with developed venture capital markets, carbon pilot cities, and projects using bond funds as capital. Executive green background further strengthens firms’ innovation response. These findings show how place-based public investment transforms fiscal allocation into corporate climate cognition and green innovation.

title: Factors influencing the formation and development of intellectual capital in agricultural enterprises
summary: The article examines the theoretical and practical aspects of forming and developing intellectual capital in agricultural enterprises amid digital transformation, technological change, and increased external uncertainty. It is shown that traditional production factors, including land, financial, and material and technical resources, are complemented by intellectual resources that enable enterprises to generate, accumulate, disseminate, and use knowledge. The text summarizes scientific approaches to defining the structure of intellectual capital, distinguishing its human, structural, and relational components. It establishes that their formation and effective use depend on the interaction of external and internal conditions in which an enterprise operates. The factors influencing intellectual capital are systematized at five levels: macroeconomic, institutional, sectoral, organizational, and individual. Macroeconomic conditions shape the general environment in which agricultural enterprises operate, while institutional factors set the rules, incentives, and constraints that affect the development of knowledge and intangible assets. The sectoral level reflects the specific characteristics of agricultural production, technological changes, natural and climatic conditions, and interactions among participants in agri-food value chains. At the enterprise level, organizational culture, management systems, investment in employee training, digitalization, innovation activity, and knowledge sharing are particularly important. The individual level encompasses education, experience, motivation, professional competencies, and employees’ ability to learn. Intellectual capital formation depends not on the isolated influence of individual factors but on their coordinated interaction. The study identifies the role of vertical relationships between levels and horizontal interaction among the components of intellectual capital. Transforming individual knowledge into an organizational resource requires appropriate management practices and partnerships throughout business activities. The practical significance of the findings lies in applying the proposed approach to comprehensively assess the conditions for intellectual capital development, identify knowledge-management priorities, and enhance the adaptability of agricultural enterprises. Keywords: intellectual capital, agricultural enterprises, human capital, structural capital, relational capital, development factors, digitalization, knowledge management, innovative development, agricultural sector.

title: Enhancing Public Accountability through IPSAS-Based Financial Reporting: Evidence from the Turkish Court of Accounts
summary: The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether financial reporting compliant with Public Accounting Standards prepared based on IPSAS enhances accountability in the public sector, through the perceptions of auditors at the Turkish Court of Accounts (TCA). Reform approaches such as new public management and new public financial management have accelerated the transition to the accrual basis in public accounting and the development of International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS). In line with this global trend, Türkiye transitioned to an accrual-based accounting system under the Public Financial Management and Control Law No. 5018, and subsequently published the Public Accounting Standards prepared based on IPSAS. Data were collected via a survey administered between March and July 2021 to 111 professional auditors at the TCA and analyzed using exploratory factor analysis and multiple linear regression. The empirical findings indicate that, according to TCA auditor perceptions, standards-compliant financial reporting is positively associated with accountability. However, the perception that full compliance with PAS had not yet been achieved in public institutions during the 2021 data collection period indicates an implementation gap between the potential benefits of the standards and the level of implementation during the reform process.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Supply Chain Management.
summary: This paper investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in supply chain management, highlighting the main challenges and opportunities of its application and developing recommendations for practice. It adopts a qualitative method, an interpretivist philosophy and a deductive approach. Primary data were collected through open-ended interviews with nineteen supply chain managers and analysed using narrative analysis. Secondary data were drawn from peer-reviewed journal articles published since 2012 and analysed thematically. The findings indicate that AI is steadily taking a larger role in the supply chain, improving the accuracy of demand forecasting and order fulfilment. AI-enabled robots and machines also reduce human error and improve workplace safety. However, the energy and cost involved can raise operational investment, and many developers are deterred by the power demands of deep learning. Introducing systems to the workforce early, with equal training for everyone, can significantly speed up adoption. This paper is condensed from an MSc applied dissertation completed at the University of Salford (2021/2022), supervised by Dr Langes Supramaniam.

title: The Transformation of Da'wah in the Digital Era: An Analysis of FoMO Culture in the Dissemination and Reception of Islamic Messages
summary: The rapid development of digital technology has transformed da'wah practices by expanding the dissemination of Islamic messages through social media, digital platforms, and networked communication environments. Alongside this transformation, Fear of Missing Out (FoMO) has emerged as a prominent feature of digital culture, influencing how individuals engage with, disseminate, and receive information online. This study aimed to analyze the transformation of da'wah in the digital era and examine the role of FoMO culture in shaping the dissemination and reception of Islamic messages within social media ecosystems. The study employed a qualitative literature review approach using a narrative-integrative review design. Data were collected from peer-reviewed journal articles, books, conference proceedings, and scholarly publications published between 2015 and 2026. Relevant literature was identified through major academic databases and analyzed using thematic analysis to identify recurring themes, patterns, and relationships across studies. The findings indicate that digital transformation has shifted da'wah from conventional face-to-face communication toward interactive, algorithm-driven, and socially networked communication practices. FoMO culture was found to increase audience engagement with Islamic content by encouraging continuous connectivity, information-seeking behavior, content sharing, and participation in online religious discussions. However, FoMO also contributes to challenges such as content simplification, misinformation, polarization, and fragmented religious understanding. Furthermore, audience reception of Islamic messages is increasingly influenced by social validation, algorithmic visibility, and trend-driven engagement. The study concludes that FoMO functions as a significant mediating factor between digital communication technologies and contemporary Islamic communication practices. These findings contribute to digital religion and Islamic communication studies while providing insights for developing effective, ethical, and audience-centered digital da'wah strategies.

title: Contributing to SDGs 9, 16, and 17: Unveiling the Role of Supply Chain Analytics, Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management and Trust
summary: ABSTRACT The primary objective of this study is to explore the relationships between supply chain (SC) analytics, cybersecurity supply chain risk management (C‐SCRM), SC trust, and Sustainable Development goals (SDGs) in a sample of Jordanian pharmaceutical SCs, considered an emerging country. To test the aforementioned relationships, a conceptual research model was designed to frame these relationships based on both information processing theory (IPT) and dynamic capabilities view (DCV). To empirically test the model, a questionnaire was developed and distributed as a measurement tool. Based on 224 responses, the data were analyzed using partial least squares‐structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM). It was concluded that the hypotheses were acceptable, that SC analytics positively impacts C‐SCRM, and that C‐SCRM positively impacts SDGs. Finally, the moderating effect of SC trust on the relationship between SC analytics and C‐SCRM was accepted. This study made interesting and meaningful academic and managerial contributions, as well as new, innovative, and fresh insights into how data analytics and cyber risk management systems can be applied in SCs and how these factors can enhance sustainable development.

title: Provincial Carbon Inequality and the Effectiveness of Green Finance Development in China
summary: ABSTRACT Development disparities within regions cause carbon inequality (CI), which exacerbates the Chinese unbalanced development problem. However, there is still a lack of research that measures CI from the aspect of intra‐regional differences and examines its impact factors. Using sub‐provincial data covering 420 cities, counties, and districts, this study measures CI in 30 Chinese provinces and investigates the influence of green finance (GF) on CI and the role of climate risk (CR) in the GF‐CI linkage. Several findings have been found. First, using the population‐weighted Williamson index to capture intra‐provincial disparities, our analysis reveals pronounced regional variation in CI, with the East and Middle regions following a U‐shaped pattern between 2008 and 2017, while the West experiences a consistent decline. Second, the dynamic panel analysis reveals that GF can reduce CI, particularly in midwestern regions and provinces characterised by lower carbon intensity. Third, the moderating effect demonstrates that climate risk (CR) weakens the inhibitory role of GF on CI. Under low CR, GF mitigates CI, whereas when CR exceeds a critical threshold, the beneficial effect of GF is reversed. This study contributes empirical insights for policymakers seeking to mitigate CI through financial instruments.

title: Business Continuity and Climate Change: Firms’ Risk Perceptions and Adaptive Measures
summary: Climate change-related hazards are increasingly affecting the physical assets, production processes, and supply chains of industrial enterprises. This study aims to evaluate the impacts of climate change-related hazards on business continuity in firms operating within OIZs as part of the RESMAR Project. As part of the research, a survey was conducted among firms operating in nine OIZs located in the Marmara Region, and the data obtained were analysed. The findings indicate that there are no statistically significant sectoral differences in firms' levels of exposure to climate change-related hazards. Instead, firms' geographical location, the infrastructure capacity of the OIZs in which they operate, and their dependence on supply chains emerged as the primary determinants of climate-related impacts. Firms operating in labour-intensive industries, such as the textile sector, and those in high-technology industries, such as the defence sector, were found to exhibit greater sensitivity to climate change. These findings highlight the need for climate change adaptation strategies in industrial enterprises to extend beyond facility-level risk management and incorporate measures aimed at strengthening supply chain resilience and enhancing the climate resilience of OIZ infrastructure.

title: Green Innovation: The Key Role of Ecopreneurs in the Development of Sustainable Technologies
summary: Introduction: Green innovation plays a pivotal role in addressing environmental challenges while fostering economic growth. As global concerns over climate change and resource depletion rise, sustainable technologies have become integral to the future of industries and society. Ecopreneurs, individuals who merge entrepreneurial spirit with environmental responsibility, are at the forefront of this transformative movement. Their ability to introduce innovative solutions that minimize environmental impact and promote sustainable practices is reshaping industries across the globe. Methodology: This study employs a qualitative research approach to explore the role of ecopreneurs in the development of sustainable technologies, using a multiple case study design to analyze their strategies, challenges and contributions. Data are gathered through semi-structured interviews with ecopreneurs, industry experts and policymakers; a structured questionnaire distributed among ecopreneurs; document analysis of publicly available reports, business case studies and academic literature; and direct or virtual observation of ecopreneurial enterprises. A purposive sampling technique selects ecopreneurs actively engaged in developing sustainable technologies, with the sample including startups, SMEs and large-scale green businesses from renewable energy, waste management and sustainable agriculture. A mixed-methods analysis combines quantitative surveys of 329 participants from urban and suburban areas with qualitative focus group discussions. Results & Discussion: Survey data from 329 participants were analysed using descriptive statistics to summarise demographic information and key variables, regression analysis to examine the strength and significance of the relationship between green messaging components and consumer behaviour, and structural equation modelling to assess the complex interactions among multiple variables. Focus group discussions provided deeper insights into consumer perceptions, with thematic analysis identifying key themes on consumer awareness and attitudes toward green marketing, the influence of eco-friendly messaging on purchasing decisions, and perceived credibility and trust in sustainable branding. Preliminary findings reveal that emotionally appealing and credible messages significantly enhance consumer intention to adopt sustainable energy solutions, while clarity in messaging was identified as a crucial factor in fostering long-term commitment to eco-friendly practices. Ecopreneurs are fundamental to the development of sustainable technologies, pioneering new products and processes where traditional industries may be slow to adapt due to short-term profit motives or resource constraints. Conclusion: Ecopreneurs are fundamental to the development of sustainable technologies, often pioneering new products, processes and solutions aimed at solving critical environmental challenges. A large portion of the green technologies developed by ecopreneurs is centred around improving resource efficiency and reducing waste, including innovations in renewable energy, waste management, water conservation and energy efficiency. The study offers actionable insights for policymakers and marketers to design effective communication strategies that resonate with diverse consumer segments, and its practical implications extend to businesses, investors and consumers, helping shape strategies, policies and practices that support sustainable technological advancements and foster an environment conducive to ecopreneur success.

title: Catalysts for Green Innovation: The Role of NGOs in India Fostering Ecopreneurship
summary: Introduction: Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs) play a crucial role in promoting sustainable development by fostering ecopreneurship — entrepreneurial ventures driven by environmental responsibility. The rise of environmental concerns has propelled the need for sustainable business models, and NGOs have emerged as vital enablers of ecopreneurship in India by providing financial assistance, technical expertise, and networking opportunities. This study examines the impact of NGOs on ecopreneurship in India by analyzing their financial support, skill development initiatives, and policy advocacy efforts. Methodology: This study adopts a mixed-methods approach, combining qualitative and quantitative data to assess the impact of NGOs on ecopreneurship. Primary data was collected through structured questionnaires distributed to 150 ecopreneurs associated with various NGOs, while secondary data was gathered from NGO reports, policy documents and academic research. A purposive sampling technique was used to select ecopreneurs who have received support from NGOs in India. Quantitative data was analyzed using statistical methods such as regression analysis and correlation tests, while qualitative insights were drawn from interviews and case studies. The study is grounded in the Triple Bottom Line framework, which evaluates business success based on economic, environmental and social performance, and covers sectors such as renewable energy, waste management, sustainable agriculture and eco-tourism. Results & Discussion: Hypothesis testing confirmed a strong positive correlation between NGO support and the success of ecopreneurial ventures. Financial support recorded a mean of 3.8 with a standard deviation of 1.2 and a correlation coefficient of 0.68 (p = 0.001); skill development a mean of 4.2, standard deviation 1.1 and correlation of 0.72 (p = 0.002); and policy advocacy a mean of 3.5, standard deviation 1.3 and correlation of 0.65 (p = 0.005). Regarding barriers, financial constraints were reported by 60% of respondents with an impact score of 4.1 (p = 0.003), bureaucratic hurdles by 55% with a score of 3.9 (p = 0.007), and lack of awareness by 45% with a score of 3.7 (p = 0.015). On skill development, technical training recorded 70% participation with an effectiveness score of 4.5 (p = 0.002), financial literacy 65% with 4.2 (p = 0.004), and market access support 60% with 4.0 (p = 0.006). All three hypotheses were therefore supported. Conclusion: NGOs play a crucial role in fostering ecopreneurship by offering financial aid, technical expertise, and market linkages. The study confirms that NGOs significantly contribute to ecopreneurial success by providing funding, capacity building and policy advocacy. Despite their contributions, challenges such as funding shortages and policy gaps persist, and financial constraints and bureaucratic hurdles limit their effectiveness. Addressing these issues can enhance the effectiveness of NGOs in promoting green innovation in India. Strengthening policy frameworks and increasing governmental collaboration can enhance NGO support mechanisms, and the study recommends policy enhancements to strengthen NGO-ecopreneur partnerships for a greener economy.

title: Development of integrated supply chains and digitalization of agricultural product sales channels
summary: The article provides a theoretical overview of the determinants of agri-food supply chain integration and develops a conceptual multi-level model for the digitalization of agricultural product sales channels. It shows that traditional linear distribution channels have exhausted their adaptive capacity amid geopolitical turbulence, climate risks, and rising transaction costs. To address the systemic exclusion of primary agricultural producers from value creation, the article proposes a transition to cyber-physical supply chains based on Industry 4.0 technologies. The article substantiates the economic impact of structural market disintermediation achieved through B2B agricultural exchanges, Short Food Supply Chain (SFSC) services, and logistics aggregators. The study outlines a synergistic technology stack: IoT sensors ensure continuous quality control and reduce physical raw material losses by 20–35%; blockchain and smart contracts optimize fund deposits via escrow, eliminating non-payment risk; and artificial intelligence algorithms enable predictive pricing and dynamic routing. The study finds that digitalizing sales channels reduces transaction costs by 15–25%, accelerates capital turnover by 4–8 times, cuts transport downtime by 40–50%, and increases selling prices for farmers by 7–15%. The paper focuses on Ukraine’s agricultural logistics under martial law, the redirection of export flows to Danube ports and western border crossings, and the role of the State Agrarian Registry (SAR) and the “eQueue” system in restoring export potential. A conceptual five-level model of the digital lifecycle of agricultural supply (“from field to settlement”) has been developed; this model minimizes the human factor, expands small businesses’ access to international markets, ensures transparent certification of grain batches, and lays the groundwork for the full integration of the domestic agricultural sector into the European Union’s single digital economic space.
