title: Structural changes in the labor market under digital transformation
summary: The article examines the digital transformation of the Ukrainian labor market. It clarifies the concept by defining it as a systemic process of qualitative changes in the structure, functioning mechanisms, and interactions among labor market actors, driven by the adoption and diffusion of digital technologies. The study analyses how digital changes have been reflected in Ukraine’s strategic and regulatory documents. The study identifies a gradual broadening of the government’s approach to these issues, ranging from considering individual components of digital development to incorporating them comprehensively into national employment policy. This chapter synthesizes contemporary scholarly approaches to transformations in employment, work organization, occupational structure, regulatory mechanisms, and workforce requirements. The paper justifies systematizing digital changes in the labor market into six interrelated dimensions. The paper specifies the content of each dimension and shows that considering them together provides a comprehensive framework for characterizing government priorities for labor market development, regulatory mechanisms, the digital infrastructure that supports them, transformations in employment forms and occupational structure, and changing competency requirements for workers. The proposed systematization complements existing scholarly approaches to studying digital transformation in labor markets. It provides a theoretical foundation for identifying interrelationships among the distinguished dimensions, assessing the nature and intensity of the corresponding changes, and developing quantitative and qualitative indicators. The findings can support a comprehensive analysis of the labor market’s digital development, assess the nature and interrelationships of the identified changes, and identify priority areas for adaptation to technological transformations and evolving conditions of economic activity. title: Sustainable Supply Chain Management Practices and Organizational Performance of Public Institutions in Rwanda: A Case of Kigali City
summary: Despite numerous efforts made by Kigali City as a public institution through the management of the use of sustainable supply chain management in terms of sustainable sourcing, green recycling, and clean energy efficiency, the performance remains critical and inadequate. Therefore, the general objective of this research project was to analyze the effect of sustainable supply chain management practices on the organizational performance of public institutions in Rwanda. The following were the three specific objectives of the study: To examine the examine the influence of sustainable sourcing on performance of Kigali City; to analyze the effect of green recycling on performance of Kigali City, to analyze the influence of clean energy efficient on performance of Kigali City as well as to analyze the effect of transportation and urban on performance of Kigali City. To achieve these objectives, literature was reviewed on the subject matter, and two theories was aligned with this research, including resource dependency theory as well as theory of empowerment. Data was collected from 138 employees of Kigali City and they were chosen by using the census sampling technique. Questionnaires, interview guides, and documentation were used as tools for data collection. The data was analyzed using both descriptive and inferential statistics by presenting the findings of respondents through the mean and standard deviation. Findings indicated that holding all the stakeholders management to a constant zero, rehousing project performance will be -.889 percent, a unit increase in the use of sustainable sourcing would lead to increase the performance of City of Kigali at 41.7%, a one percent increase in the use of green recycling would lead the performance of City of Kigali at 61.1%, a one percent increase in the use of clean energy efficient would lead to an increase the performance of City of Kigali at 61.1%, furthermore a one percentage increase in the use of transport and urban planning would lead to 22.2% increase the performance of City of Kigali. Overall, both the Green recycling and Clean energy efficient had the greatest effect on the performance of City of Kigali, followed by sustainable sourcing, as well as transport and urban planning. At 5% level of significance and 95% level of confidence, transport and urban planning had 0.048 level of significance; green recycling had a 0.002 level of significance, sustainable sourcing had a 0.004 level of significance and finally clean energy efficient had 0.007 level of significance.

title: The Church as a Feeding Community in Acts 2:42-47 And its Implications for Corporate Social Responsibility in the Redeemed Christian Church of God, Ogun State, Nigeria
summary: Abstract The duty of the Church extends beyond spiritual teachings such as personal transformation, financial upliftment, moral growth and human behaviour. The New Testament emphasizes the Church’s role in responding to people’s needs, as depicted in Acts 2:42-47. However, the Church’s response to these social issues has been the subject of debate among scholars. Hence, this study examined the role of the Church as a feeding community in Acts 2:42-47 and its implications for corporate social responsibility (CSR) in the Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG), Ogun State. The study employed a mixed-methods approach that included a descriptive survey and a historical-critical hermeneutical approach. While the survey used a questionnaire to gather information from respondents, content analysis was used to analyze the biblical text under study. The study population comprised all members of the RCCG in two LGAs of Ogun State. 300 respondents were selected using a stratified sampling technique. Secondary data were drawn from Acts 2:42-47, and the study employed a self-administered, unstructured questionnaire for primary data collection. Findings revealed that although the RCCG has demonstrated acts of kindness by engaging in various CSR initiatives to address poverty, food insecurity, lack of education, among others, these initiatives have not addressed the aforementioned social challenges. Thus, the study recommended, among others, that the RCCG should prioritize personal growth over the distribution of unsustainable material aid. Also, the church should establish microfinance banks across Nigeria that can facilitate loans at low interest rates. Keywords: Acts 2:42-47, corporate social responsibility, feeding community, RCCG

title: Determinants of Key Audit Matters (KAMs) Disclosure: Empirical Evidence from an Emerging Economy
summary: The introduction of new audit requirements regarding the disclosure of KAMs enhances the communicational value of audit reports. Therefore, the objectives of this study are to examine the impact of auditors’ characteristics and corporate governance characteristics on key audit matters (KAMs) disclosure in auditors’ report in an emerging economy like Bangladesh. Herein, DS30 companies listed in DSE from 2018 to 2023 are taken as a sample because it starts after the mandatory implementation of ISA 701 and KAM reporting requirements in Bangladesh and provides enough time to observe meaningful changes in KAM disclosure practices. Using a multivariate pooled OLS regression analysis, this study finds significant positive association of auditors’ attributes (BIG4, FEMA, AFEE and ATENURE) on disclosure of KAMs. Additionally, among the corporate governance characteristics BIND and ACIND have significant positive impacts on the disclosure of KAMs whereas ACEXP has significant negative effect on the disclosure of KAMs. This study additionally reinforces the significance of women’s involvement in the growth of emerging economies and emphasizes the value of women’s engagement and ongoing professional development. Thus, the findings of the study contribute to Agency Theory, Resource Dependence Theory and Upper Echelons Theory by showing how auditor and governance characteristics influence KAM disclosure through monitoring, resource, and judgement-based mechanisms. The study’s findings also assist standard-setters, regulators, and those who produce financial statements by giving them a better knowledge of the factors that could influence a decision to report KAMs by an auditor. However, new areas for future research could include the perception of new regulations by auditors, the strength of auditors’ resources, the presence of women in senior management, the interaction between female auditors and female audit committee members, as well as family ownership.

title: From Microscope to Monitor: The Digital Transformation of Veterinary Pathology
summary: Pathology has traditionally been synonymous with the microscope, glass slides and the trained eye of the pathologist. However, advances in imaging technology, computing and artificial intelligence are transforming this conventional approach. Digital pathology involves converting glass microscope slides into high-resolution digital images that can be viewed, stored, analysed and shared electronically. In veterinary medicine, this technology has applications in diagnosis, telepathology, education, research, disease surveillance and quantitative image analysis. Whole-slide imaging allows an entire tissue section to be examined on a computer screen, while artificial intelligence and machine-learning tools are opening new possibilities for automated image analysis and computer-assisted diagnosis. At the same time, challenges related to infrastructure, cost, data storage, standardisation, validation and cybersecurity need to be addressed. Digital pathology is therefore not simply a replacement for the microscope; rather, it represents an evolution of pathology that can extend the reach and capabilities of veterinary pathologists.

title: Pengaruh Ukuran Perusahaan, Ukuran Kantor Akuntan Publik (KAP) dan Profitabilitas terhadap Audit Delay pada Emiten LQ45 yang Terdaftar di Bursa Efek Indonesia Tahun 2023 – 2024
summary: This study aims to examine the effect of company size, Public Accounting Firm size, and profitability on audit delay in companies listed in the LQ45 index on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) for the 2023–2024 period. The research method used is a quantitative approach with a purposive sampling technique, resulting in 90 observations from audited financial statements. Data were analyzed using multiple linear regression with the classical assumption test. The results of the study indicate that company size and Public Accounting Firm size negatively and significantly affect audit delay. This means that the larger the company size and if the company is audited by a Public Accounting Firm affiliated with the Big Four, the shorter the audit delay time will be. However, profitability does not affect audit delay. This finding provides implications for companies with high or low profitability values to still go through the audit process in accordance with applicable provisions. This study contributes recent empirical evidence from LQ45 issuers for 2023–2024, showing that audit delay is more closely associated with firm size and public accounting firm size than with profitability, thereby enriching evidence on the determinants of audit timeliness in the Indonesian capital market. title: Process–project model of management cost accounting in construction enterprises
summary: The article substantiates the organizational and methodological foundations of a process–project model of management cost accounting for construction enterprises aimed at overcoming the information gap between project costing, process-based resource consumption, and responsibility centres. Systems and process approaches, as well as methods of classification, comparison, grouping, and structural-logical modelling, are applied. A system of internal indicators is developed to ensure a consistent link between business transactions, consumed resources, business processes, construction projects, work stages, and responsibility centres. Rules for the direct attribution of costs and the causal allocation of indirect costs using appropriate cost drivers are substantiated. A “business process – construction project” matrix is proposed, enabling both the analysis of an individual project’s cost structure by process and the comparison of identical process costs across projects. An internal reporting format is developed to compare budgeted costs, flexible standards for actual output, and actual costs, while identifying the causes of variances, responsible persons, and corrective management actions. The scientific novelty lies in integrating project costing, process accounting, causal cost allocation, and responsibility control into a unified information model. The model is extended by incorporating environmental cost drivers and ESG indicators related to material circularity, resource reuse, waste management, and resource and energy efficiency. Its practical value lies in improving the accuracy of cost allocation, the timeliness of cost control, and the validity of management decisions, while providing an information basis for ESG reporting without establishing a parallel accounting system. Keywords: management accounting; construction costs; business process; construction project; responsibility center; cost factor; variance analysis; management reporting; circular economy; ESG.

title: Digital Transformation in Banking and Financial Performance of Commercial Banks in Uasin Gishu County, Kenya.
summary: Digital banking adoption refers to the integration and use of electronic platforms such as mobile banking, internet banking, agency banking and automated teller machines (ATMs) to deliver financial services. It is increasingly regarded as a critical driver of efficiency, service delivery and financial performance in the banking sector. Global evidence shows that digital banking usage exceeds 70% in advanced markets, while in Kenya over 80% of banking transactions are now conducted through digital channels. However, financial performance across commercial banks remains uneven owing to disparities in digital infrastructure, cybersecurity risks, high technology investment costs and uneven adoption across institutions, and existing studies provide limited localized evidence on how specific digital channels influence financial performance. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to examine the effect of digital transformation in banking on the financial performance of commercial banks in Uasin Gishu County, Kenya. It specifically assessed the influence of mobile banking adoption, internet banking adoption, agency banking adoption and ATM adoption on financial performance measured through return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE) and net interest margin (NIM). The study was anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model, Diffusion of Innovation Theory, Resource-Based View and Transaction Cost Theory. The study adopted a longitudinal panel research design and targeted the 39 licensed commercial banks in Kenya. A purposive sample of 12 commercial banks with complete records was observed over the period 2018–2025, yielding 96 bank-year observations. Secondary data were obtained from Central Bank of Kenya reports, audited financial statements and annual bank reports using a structured data extraction sheet. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and panel regression analysis in STATA version 17.0, supported by diagnostic and model specification tests, and the random effects model was selected on the basis of the Hausman test. The findings revealed that the four digital banking channels jointly explained 78.0% of the variation in financial performance. Mobile banking adoption had the strongest positive and significant effect on financial performance, followed by internet banking adoption, agency banking adoption and ATM adoption, all of which had positive and significant effects. The study therefore recommends that commercial banks should enhance mobile banking platforms through improved usability, reliability and cybersecurity; strengthen and integrate internet banking systems; expand agency banking networks while improving agent support and service quality; and modernize ATM infrastructure and integrate it with other digital channels.

title: The Decision Architecture of Supply Chain Management: Separating Decisions, Solutions, Evidence, and Context
summary: Supply-chain management (SCM) research is analytically rich but representationally fragmented: studies are often identified by technology, method, industry, objective, or risk domain even when these descriptors refer to different aspects of the underlying managerial decision. This paper develops and evaluates the Supply Chain Decision Architecture (SCDA), which separates a four-dimensional Decision Kernel from Solution, Evidence, and Context layers. A reproducible review pipeline identified 705 unique candidate records; 659 advanced to Stage-2 screening and 518 were retained. A prespecified deep-review corpus contained 125 studies, including 121 primary analytical studies yielding 124 source-supported claims. Independent second-coder review showed heterogeneous agreement across the nine dimensions (Cohen’s κ = 0.036–0.712). Coder-sensitivity analysis nevertheless showed a consistent K4→KS7→KSV8→SCDA9 reduction in collision under both independent codings, although absolute collision levels differed substantially. Repeated 80/20 record-level holdouts further showed that preferred depth was coder- and sample-sensitive rather than universally fixed. In the frozen 124-claim analysis, collision decreased from 52.42% for K4 to 19.35% for KS7, 17.74% for KSV8, and 12.90% for SCDA9. The primary τ = 0.02 specification selected SCDA9, whereas a looser τ = 0.05 selected KSV8 and the original 24-study publication holdout selected KS7. A permutation diagnostic further showed that arbitrary independently permuted fields can reduce collision mechanically; collision is therefore interpreted only as within-corpus discriminability, not ontology validity. The evidence supports a layered decision-and-solution representation while treating outer-layer necessity as contingent on coding, sample composition, and analytical purpose.

title: Lifelong Learning in the Context of Digital Transformation: The Changing Role of Universities
summary: Digital transformation is reshaping the conditions under which universities organize education, recognize learning, and engage with society. Although higher education has traditionally focused on degree programmes undertaken during early adulthood, contemporary technological and social changes require educational opportunities across the life course. This conceptual article examines the relationship between digital transformation, lifelong learning, and the changing role of universities. Drawing on selected scholarly publications and international policy documents, it argues that meaningful transformation requires more than the adoption of digital platforms. Universities need coordinated institutional arrangements that support flexible participation, recognition of prior learning, inclusive pedagogy, ethical technological practices, and sustained community engagement. The article proposes a framework comprising five interconnected dimensions: access, support, recognition, governance, and public value. It also examines tensions between employability and broader educational purposes, flexibility and credential fragmentation, and technological personalization and learner autonomy. The central argument is that universities should approach lifelong learning as an institution-wide educational responsibility. Digital transformation should consequently be evaluated through learning quality, equitable participation, and social contribution, alongside operational efficiency. The article concludes with recommendations for institutional development and directions for empirical research.

title: Pengaruh Good Corporate Governance dan Intellectual Capital Terhadap Kinerja Keuangan pada IDX30 yang terdaftar di Bursa Efek Indonesia
summary: ABSTRACT This study looks at how intellectual capital and sound corporate governance affect the financial performance of companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange's IDX30 index between 2022 and 2024. Using a purposive sampling technique, non-financial businesses that were included in the IDX30 index for at least two consecutive periods and submitted fully audited annual reports were chosen. This produced a sample of 16 businesses that were monitored throughout a three-year period, giving a total of 48 data points. Return on Assets (ROA) reflected financial performance, intellectual capital was measured using the Value Added Intellectual Coefficient (VAIC) technique, and the percentage of independent commissioners acted as a stand-in for sound corporate governance. Multiple linear regression, classical assumption tests, and hypothesis testing (t-test and F-test) utilizing SPSS software were used for the analysis. According to the findings, effective corporate governance had a coefficient of -0.134 and a significance level of 0.211 (>0.05), indicating that it had no discernible impact on financial performance. On the other hand, intellectual capital demonstrated a positive and significant impact on financial performance with a coefficient of 0.019 and a significance level of 0.000 (<0.05). With an R2 value of 0.379, effective corporate governance and intellectual capital had a substantial impact on financial success when examined concurrently. This means that the two factors together accounted for 37.9% of the observed variation in financial performance. Keywords: Good Corporate Governance, Intellectual Capital, Financial Performance. ABSTRAK Penelitian ini mengkaji bagaimana modal intelektual dan tata kelola perusahaan yang baik memengaruhi kinerja keuangan perusahaan yang terdaftar dalam indeks IDX30 Bursa Efek Indonesia antara tahun 2022 dan 2024. Perusahaan sektor non-keuangan yang secara konsisten masuk dalam indeks IDX30 selama setidaknya dua periode berturut-turut dan memiliki laporan tahunan teraudit yang lengkap dipilih menggunakan teknik purposive sampling; proses ini menghasilkan sampel sebanyak 16 perusahaan yang diamati selama tiga tahun, sehingga diperoleh total 48 observasi. Kinerja keuangan diukur menggunakan Return on Assets (ROA), tata kelola perusahaan yang baik direpresentasikan oleh persentase komisaris independen, dan modal intelektual diukur menggunakan pendekatan Value Added Intellectual Coefficient (VAIC). title: Unplanned Urbanisation and the Right to a Healthy Environment: Rethinking Environmental Governance in Himachal Pradesh
summary: Abstract Himachal Pradesh presents an unusually demanding setting for environmental governance because urban growth takes place on steep, geologically fragile and disaster-prone terrain while being driven by tourism, transport infrastructure, housing demand and expanding commercial activity. The resulting legal problem is not simply whether individual projects comply with environmental statutes, but whether the cumulative pattern of urbanisation is compatible with the constitutional obligation to secure a healthy environment. This article examines the relationship between unplanned urbanisation and the right to a healthy environment in Himachal Pradesh, with particular attention to Shimla and the wider Himalayan urban context. It argues that Indian environmental law has already developed the constitutional and doctrinal foundations necessary for an integrated model of ecological urban governance, but those foundations remain institutionally fragmented. Town planning, municipal regulation, environmental clearance, forest protection, disaster management, waste regulation and climate adaptation are commonly administered through separate legal channels even though they operate on the same ecological system. The article analyses Article 21, Articles 47, 48A and 51A(g), the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, the Himachal Pradesh Town and Country Planning Act 1977, municipal legislation, the Environmental Impact Assessment framework and the jurisprudence of the Supreme Court and National Green Tribunal. It particularly examines the Supreme Court's decisions in State of Himachal Pradesh v Yogendera Mohan Sengupta (2024) and M/s Pristine Hotels and Resorts Pvt Ltd v State of Himachal Pradesh (2025), alongside the continuing judicial scrutiny of Himachal's ecological condition. The article proposes a framework of ecological urban governance based on carrying capacity, risk-sensitive zoning, cumulative impact assessment, climate-resilient planning, transparent environmental data, meaningful public participation and enforceable development controls. It concludes that the right to a healthy environment should operate not merely as a remedial right after pollution or disaster occurs, but as a substantive planning principle governing where, how and at what intensity urban development may lawfully occur in a fragile Himalayan state.

title: The digital transformation paradox: how organizational and institutional barriers neutralize leadership investment in systemic banking
summary: Purpose This study examines the “digital transformation paradox” in which systemic banks invest heavily in technology yet remain digitally immature. It identifies and prioritizes the key technological, organizational, and institutional barriers that constrain transformation despite strong leadership commitment. Ultimately, the paper reframes digital transformation from a problem of execution to a problem of institutional design. Design/methodology/approach The study applies a hybrid Delphi–scaling methodology with senior experts from Greece’s four systemic banks. It integrates Institutional Theory with an extended Technology–Organization–Environment–Value (TOE–V) framework. A Delphi process established consensus on 14 major inhibitors, followed by a scaling survey that ranked their relative impact. Findings The results reveal a persistent transformation trap driven by legacy information technology (IT) systems, rigid organizational routines, and compliance-focused governance. These factors redirect modernization toward regulatory conformity rather than operational improvement. Clear and enforceable regulatory mandates, however, can act as catalysts for modernization. Digital maturity should be assessed not only in terms of adoption but also in terms of outcomes, including usability, personalisation, and relevance to stakeholders. Practical implications Executives should move beyond viewing transformation as primarily a technology initiative and address structural constraints such as technical debt and cultural resistance, and tie digital investments to measurable stakeholder outcomes. Originality/value The study conceptualizes the digital transformation paradox as a systemic outcome of organizational and institutional constraints. It extends the TOE framework through TOE–V by showing how value realization conditions digital maturity in regulated environments, repositioning digital transformation as a challenge of institutional design rather than execution.

title: Drug shortages in Italy: strategic insights and empirical evidence from the Italian pharmaceutical market
summary: Abstract Drug shortages disrupt healthcare delivery and pose a critical challenge to the resilience of pharmaceutical supply chains. This study investigates the drivers of drug shortages in Italy – Europe’s leading pharmaceutical producer – to identify the factors associated with supply disruptions and inform evidence-based health policy. Using national data from 2018 to 2023, we analysed 17,619 drugs across 3,013 groups of substitutes, covering community , dual-dispensed , and hospital distribution channels. Generalised linear mixed models were employed to assess how drug characteristics, market dynamics, and regulatory features influence shortage risk. Shortages were most prevalent among community drugs, where high market fragmentation and low-profit margins contributed to supply instability. Patent protection was associated with lower shortage risk for non-sterile drugs, while sterile drugs remained vulnerable regardless of patent status, likely due to manufacturing complexity. Notably, price effects were age-dependent: higher prices mitigated shortage risk, particularly for older drugs. This study offers a comprehensive evaluation of shortage patterns in a key pharmaceutical market, identifying structural risk factors and market vulnerabilities. The findings provide actionable insights for policymakers aiming to design targeted interventions, strengthen supply chain resilience, and ensure continuous access to essential medicines.

title: Capital expenditure and sustainability performance among listed firms in Ghana: the mediating role of ESG disclosure quality
summary: Abstract The study investigates the relationship between capital expenditure, ESG disclosure quality, and sustainability performance, with a particular focus on the mediating role of ESG disclosure quality. The data cover 18 firms listed on the Ghana Stock Exchange from 2010 to 2024. The study utilizes the two-step System GMM and Sobel test mediation approach to analyze the study objective. The results reveal a positive and statistically significant association between capital expenditure and sustainability performance, as well as between capital expenditure and ESG disclosure quality. ESG disclosure quality is, in turn, positively associated with sustainability performance, and the Sobel test confirms a statistically significant indirect effect, supporting partial mediation. These findings extend stakeholder theory by alluding that capital budgeting decisions, not only disclosure practices, may serve as a channel for stakeholder responsiveness, and contribute to legitimacy theory by signifying that investment activity and ESG communication are statistically connected rather than independent legitimation strategies. The findings suggest that corporate entities should invest more in sustainability efforts and report on ESG issues transparently and credibly to achieve the best sustainability results. In conclusion, the study underscores the need for financial investment in sustainability and effective communication via ESG disclosures, offering insights for corporate managers and policymakers in Ghana to boost corporate sustainability practices and strengthen ESG reporting standards.

title: SUPPLY CHAIN MANAGEMENT AND THE SUSTAINABILITY OF FAMILY-OWNED SUPERMARKETS: EVIDENCE FROM KIAMBU COUNTY, KENYA
summary: Purpose of the study: The study examined the effect of supply chain management on the sustainability of family-owned supermarkets in Kiambu County, Kenya, using the Resource-Based View and Stewardship Theory. Statement of the problem: Although supply chain management is central to retail sustainability, its specific contribution among family-owned supermarkets in Sub-Saharan Africa remains insufficiently established. Existing evidence is largely drawn from manufacturing firms, large retail chains, and family businesses outside the Kenyan supermarket context. This creates limited subsector-specific evidence to guide supply chain investment decisions. Research methodology: The study adopted a pragmatist philosophy and a mixed-methods, cross-sectional survey design. Structured questionnaires were administered to 183 owners, managers, and supervisors from 70 registered family-owned supermarkets selected through multistage stratified sampling, complemented by key informant interviews. Quantitative data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling in STATA. Findings: Supply chain management recorded strong reliability and validity and a high composite mean (M = 4.22). It had a strong positive effect on sustainability (β = 0.631, t = 11.349, p < .001), explaining approximately 41.6% of the variance. Supplier diversification and communication quality were the strongest practices, while interview findings linked supplier diversification to business continuity during disruptions. Conclusion: The study concludes that supply chain management is a core operational capability supporting the sustainability of family-owned supermarkets. Supplier diversification, efficient lead-time management, and collaborative supplier relationships strengthen continuity and operational resilience. Recommendations: The study recommends deliberate investment in supplier diversification, resilience and contingency planning, and collaborative supplier relationship systems. Family-owned supermarkets should institutionalise these practices in routine strategic and operational planning. Industry associations and county business development offices should widen access to vetted regional suppliers and shared logistics infrastructure. title: Securing the open-source ecosystem: AI-enhanced and explainable supply chain security for reliable software development
summary: Abstract Modern software supply chains face increasing risks from vulnerable and anomalous dependencies, necessitating automated and interpretable detection methods integrated within Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) workflows. Open-source software (OSS) ecosystems are increasingly targeted by sophisticated attacks—including AI model poisoning, dependency confusion, contributor hijacking, and transitive dependency anomalies—that often evade traditional CVE-centric tools such as Snyk and Dependabot. These reactive solutions are primarily designed for known vulnerabilities and may exhibit high false-positive rates when applied to behavioral anomalies, while also lacking interpretable and actionable guidance for developers. This limitation creates a critical barrier to reliable and secure software development in modern DevSecOps environments. To address this gap, this paper introduces XAI-SCS, an intelligent, explainable decision-support framework for OSS supply chain security that performs metadata-driven behavioral risk assessment to proactively identify anomalous package activity. A hybrid CNN–LSTM–Autoencoder architecture achieves strong anomaly-detection performance on the held-out test set (F1 = 0.91), with low repeated-run variability (mean F1 = 0.90 ± 0.02 across five runs) on a federated dataset of 12,000 npm/PyPI package versions, primarily trained using CVE-linked labels and GAN-simulated poisoning samples. A separate held-out evaluation set of 240 manually curated real-world non-CVE OSS supply-chain incidents was used exclusively for external generalization assessment. Accordingly, the non-CVE results are interpreted as preliminary evidence of transferability to selected metadata-visible behavioral anomalies rather than comprehensive real-world non-CVE threat coverage. To support transparent developer decision-making, SHAP-based explanations and counterfactual remediation suggestions produced high perceived clarity (4.3 ± 0.4/5) and actionability (4.1 ± 0.5/5) and self-reported remediation intent (96%, n = 82). However, these findings reflect developer perceptions in a controlled study and do not yet demonstrate measured improvements in real-world remediation time, fix completion, or vulnerability resolution within operational DevSecOps teams. Optional high-assurance deployment extensions, including Federated Continual Learning, zero-knowledge attestation via zk-SNARKs, and post-quantum secure enclaves, are presented as exploratory architectural pathways for future privacy-preserving, verifiable, and confidential deployment, rather than as part of the core empirical evaluation. Embedded in controlled, CI/CD-representative workflows with 0.8-second average latency, XAI-SCS remains competitive with CVE-centric tools on known-vulnerability cases while providing preliminary evidence of complementary metadata-level behavioral risk screening in GAN-simulated and limited curated non-CVE evaluation subsets. The comparison is therefore interpreted as evidence that XAI-SCS can complement CVE-centric SCA tools by adding metadata-level behavioral screening and developer-facing explanations, rather than replacing or universally outperforming tools such as Snyk and Dependabot. This work’s primary contribution is a metadata-driven, CI/CD-integrated intelligent decision-support framework that delivers high-accuracy behavioral anomaly detection (F1 = 0.91) and transparent, developer-facing explanations (clarity 4.3/5, remediation intent 96%) for OSS supply chain risk assessment. Optional high-assurance deployment extensions (federated learning, cryptographic attestation, secure enclaves) are discussed separately and do not form part of the core empirical evaluation.

title: The financial performance of listed firms in Tanzanian Dar es Salaam stock exchange (DSE): Does the disclosure of non-financial information (NFI) matter?
summary: Non-financial information (NFI) disclosure is increasingly important in investment decision-making and corporate accountability. However, empirical evidence regarding the relationship between NFI disclosure and firm performance remains inconclusive. This study examined the relationship between NFI disclosure and the financial performance of firms listed on the Dar es Salaam Stock Exchange (DSE), guided by Legitimacy Theory and Stakeholder Theory. A mixed-methods approach using an explanatory sequential design was employed, covering 21 locally listed firms over the period 2006–2019. Panel data were analysed using the Random Effects Model, while qualitative data obtained through semi-structured interviews were analysed thematically. Firm performance was measured using Return on Assets (ROA), while NFI disclosure was represented by corporate social responsibility information, corporate governance information, and risk management information. Firm age, firm size, and geographical diversification were included as control variables. The findings indicate a positive relationship between the NFI categories and ROA. The study concludes that greater NFI disclosure is associated with improved firm performance by enhancing transparency and stakeholder confidence. It recommends that managers strengthen NFI disclosure through appropriate communication channels and that regulators enhance monitoring of compliance with applicable NFI disclosure requirements.

title: Modern slavery remediation in healthcare supply chains through blockchain implementation: a socio-technical systems perspective
summary: Purpose Modern slavery remediation remains a supply chain concern for Australian healthcare organisations, which rely heavily on imported goods with limited upstream visibility. Although blockchain is recognised as a means of enhancing supply chain transparency, little is known about how it can be effectively implemented across organisational boundaries. Taking a socio-technical systems approach, this study investigates how blockchain can support the remediation of modern slavery in healthcare supply chains. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts an abductive approach based on semi-structured interviews with healthcare procurement managers and blockchain experts. The abductive approach enables iterative engagement between theoretical insights and empirical evidence to develop a context-sensitive understanding of blockchain implementation in healthcare supply chains. Findings Blockchain implementation for modern slavery remediation is shaped by the interaction between the social and technical subsystems within a broader macro-environmental context. Healthcare organisations are motivated to implement blockchain by external accountability pressures, modern slavery data governance needs, socially sustainable procurement objectives and proactive risk management. However, implementation is constrained by socio-technical misalignments, including uneven organisational readiness, supplier integration barriers and technology-related challenges. To address these misalignments, the study identifies key enabling mechanisms, including supplier support and capability development, strategic stakeholder collaboration and organisational learning. Originality/value This study provides an early empirical investigation of buyer-initiated blockchain implementation for modern slavery remediation in Australian healthcare supply chains. Moving beyond techno-optimistic and techno-pessimistic perspectives, it demonstrates that blockchain effectiveness is neither guaranteed by technical capabilities nor constrained solely by technological limitations but depends on achieving socio-technical alignment across supply chains.

title: FROM SATYAM TO SAHARA: EVOLUTION OF ACCOUNTABILITY MECHANISMS FOR CORPORATE FRAUD IN INDIA
summary: Corporate fraud is among the most serious threats to the integrity, transparency and credibility ofthe Indian corporate sector. Fraudulent financial reporting, diversion of funds, manipulation ofaccounts, misrepresentation of financial information, insider misconduct and failures of corporategovernance harm shareholders, employees, creditors, investors and the wider economy. Thescandals involving Satyam Computer Services Ltd. and the Sahara group offer two instructivereference points for examining how India's accountability framework for corporate fraud hasevolved.The Satyam scandal of January 2009 exposed serious weaknesses in financial reporting, auditing andboard supervision, and prompted a government-led investigation, including scrutiny of the role ofindependent directors and statutory auditors. The Companies Act, 2013 subsequently introducedstronger provisions on fraud, investigation, auditor accountability, independent directors andcorporate governance, and gave statutory status to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO). TheSahara controversy, which unfolded in parallel before SEBI and the Supreme Court and later led toSFIO investigations under Section 212 of the 2013 Act, demonstrated the importance of regulatorycoordination and judicial supervision where the public at large is affected.This paper examines corporate fraud accountability in India under seven heads: (1) introduction; (2)corporate governance as an accountability mechanism; (3) corporate fraud and its forms; (4) theSatyam scandal as a turning point; (5) development of legal and institutional accountabilitymechanisms; (6) critical evaluation, challenges and suggestions; and (7) conclusion. It analyses thetransition from a predominantly reactive enforcement approach towards a framework built onprevention, disclosure, governance, supervision, investigation and judicial accountability, andevaluates the roles of SEBI, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA), SFIO, auditors, independentdirectors, stock exchanges, the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and the courts.

title: Too Much Financial Integration: The Perils of Open Capital Accounts in Low and Middle Income Countries
summary: ABSTRACT Over the past 3 decades, financial integration of lower income countries with global capital markets has in most cases been detrimental to development. Currency hierarchies determine investor perceptions and render capital flows to such countries more volatile and more demanding of higher returns. They also lead to significant spillover effects of macroeconomic policies in advanced economies. As a result, financial integration has not led to sustained increases in investment rates or economic growth, has generated greater financial instability and vulnerability, and been associated with high ‘seignorage costs’ because of differences in rates of return of capital inflows and outflows. Developing countries now suffer from ‘too much financial integration’, and cross‐border capital flows should be more regulated.

title: Artificial intelligence in risk-based auditing of large enterprise taxation
summary: The article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations for applying artificial intelligence (AI) in risk-based audits of large enterprise taxation. The study’s relevance stems from the significant fiscal role of large taxpayers, the complexity of their business transactions, the prevalence of cross-border transactions and transfer pricing practices, and the need to identify tax risks promptly amid the digital transformation of tax administration. The study aims to identify areas for AI application to improve the effectiveness of identifying, assessing, and prioritizing tax risks for large enterprises. Based on an analysis of academic research and international approaches, the study systematizes the key tax risks inherent in large enterprises, including those related to transfer pricing, profit shifting across jurisdictions, transactions involving intangible assets, intra-group financing, corporate income taxation, value-added tax (VAT), and tax compliance. The study explores the potential of machine learning, anomaly detection algorithms, predictive analytics, natural language processing (NLP), cluster analysis, and network analysis for processing large volumes of financial and tax data. This study develops a structural and logical model for applying AI in risk-based audits of large enterprise taxation, integrating information and analytical support, AI tools, tax risk profiling, and the auditor’s professional judgment. AI-driven analysis should provide an analytical basis for identifying areas of heightened tax risk and prioritizing audit procedures, while final audit decisions should remain grounded in the auditor’s professional judgment. The practical significance of the findings lies in the potential application of the proposed approach to enhance the validity and effectiveness of risk-based audits of large enterprise taxation. title: Does Digital Transformation Drive the Adjustment of Bank Loan Structure? Evidence From China
summary: ABSTRACT This article examines the impact of digital transformation on bank loan structure. We employ text mining and the entropy weight method to measure the five‐dimensional digital transformation index of banks and conduct an empirical analysis based on the panel data of 132 commercial banks in China from 2013 to 2022. The results indicate that digital transformation significantly drives the adjustment of various types of bank loan structures, increasing the proportion of unsecured loans, personal loans, medium‐ and long‐term loans, manufacturing loans, and green loans. In terms of the impact mechanism, improving information screening capability and enhancing risk control capability are two key channels through which digital transformation exerts its impact. Furthermore, the heterogeneity analysis reveals that the impact of digital transformation on loan structures varies among banks with different asset size, profitability, and management efficiency. Finally, we propose targeted suggestions for commercial banks and regulatory authorities.

title: Digitization tools as a basis for improving the accounting and taxation of an agrarian enterprise
summary: The article examines the theoretical-methodical and applied principles of digitalization of accounting and taxation in an agrarian enterprise amid increasing information volumes, more complex economic processes, and the need for operational information support for management decisions. It is substantiated that the digitalization of accounting and tax activities should be considered not only as the automation of individual operations, but as a complex process of forming an integrated information environment of the enterprise. The main digitalization tools include primary accounting, electronic document management, accounting and tax accounting, electronic reporting, digital control, analytics, and management. The peculiarities of their application in the agricultural sector are defined by production seasonality, the territorial dispersion of economic processes, the large volume of primary documents, and the need to record production data in real time. The study proposes a conceptual model for the integrated digitalization of accounting and taxation in an agrarian enterprise, establishing consistent relationships among primary accounting, electronic document flow, a single information base, accounting and tax accounting, electronic reporting, digital control, BI analytics, and management decisions, with feedback loops. The study proposes guidelines for evaluating the effectiveness of digitization based on time, quality, cost, tax, information, management, and personnel criteria. The study identifies the main risks of digital transformation and proposes a step-by-step implementation approach. The study shows that integrating digital tools improves the efficiency and reliability of accounting and tax information, reduces labor intensity and tax risks, and improves the quality of management decisions. title: Does international supply shock necessitate supply chain diversification? Evidence from China’s imports of intermediate goods
summary: This paper examines the impact of international intermediate input supply shocks on firms’ supply chain diversification and its adjustment direction. Using Chinese firm-level customs data from 2009 to 2016, we find a significant U-shaped relationship between supply shocks and supply chain diversification. When shocks are relatively weak, firms tend to maintain concentrated supply chains due to cost and efficiency considerations. Once shocks exceed a certain threshold, firms increase diversification to mitigate risks. Further analysis shows that firms adjust not only the degree but also the direction of supply chain diversification. In response to supply shocks, firms shift from efficiency-oriented to security-oriented sourcing strategies, increasing imports from countries with regional trade agreements, Belt and Road participation, and lower geopolitical risks, while reducing dependence on politically distant or disaster-prone regions. This paper reveals the dynamic trade-off underlying firms’ supply chain decisions and provides micro-level evidence for understanding how firms in emerging economies respond to global supply disruptions.

title: 19. Digital Governance and State Capacity in Africa: Institutional Challenges in Public-Sector Digital Transformation
summary: The drive towards digital transformation has been a growing part of the agenda for public-sector reform in Africa. Governments are implementing various technologies—such as digital identification systems, online public service platforms, electronic payment systems, data-sharing infrastructure, digital procurement systems, etc.—to enhance administrative efficiency, the access to and nature of public services, accountability, and state responsiveness. However, increasing the use of digital government does not necessarily lead to improved state capacity. The success of any digital transformation relies on public organisations' institutional capacity to coordinate digital transformation, fund and sustain digital infrastructure, build skills, create interoperability, secure data, oversee cybersecurity, and integrate digital investments into everyday administrative operations. The article explores the institutional challenges that explain digital transformation in the public sector in Africa, specifically by looking at the link between digital governance and state capacity. Based on evidence from the African Union, the United Nations, the World Bank, the OECD and comparative digital-government datasets, it claims that the flipside of the digitization of technologies is the decentralization of digital government within the state itself. There is persistent evidence of poor interoperability, digital skills, institutional coordination, regulatory capacity, data governance, cyber security, financing, and citizen inclusion. Meanwhile, there have been tangible advances in online service provision, digital identification, digital payments, and common digital infrastructure in Africa. This analysis thus denies a straightforward technologization deficit explanation. Rather, digital transformation is seen as an institutional-capacity challenge in which technology, administrative organisation, regulations, human resources and political coordination play a part. The article concludes that sustainable digital governance needs to foster a holistic approach to coordination among government bodies, interoperable digital public infrastructure (DPI), improved capacities of public sector, institutionalized data governance, cybersecurity capacities and tools for assessing real service use and administrative outcomes.

title: The Impact of Digital Transformation on Improving the Performance of Contemporary Political Systems: An Analytical Study in Governance and Decision-Making
summary: Government digital transformation is an ever-expanding part of modern governance. Governments increasingly implement digital platforms, big-data analytics, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, digital identity systems and integrated information infrastructures. These developments can affect the delivery of public services as well as institutional coordination, citizen–government interaction, policy formulation and decision-making. This paper explores how digital transformation affects the performance of contemporary political systems, particularly in governance and governmental decision-making. It examines the potential of digital technologies to enhance administrative efficiency, institutional responsiveness, transparency, accountability, citizen engagement and evidence-based policy-making, together with the problems of cybersecurity, privacy, digital exclusion, algorithmic bias, institutional capacity and over-reliance on technology. The study is qualitative and analytical: it reviews and synthesizes the academic literature and the reports of international organizations. Digital transformation is not simply the conversion of traditional administrative procedures into electronic processes; it is institutional change in its own right. Current studies suggest that it requires organizational transformation, sound data governance, interoperability, an adequate legal framework, public-sector skills and accountability mechanisms. Mergel, Edelmann and Haug argue that digital transformation is not merely digitization but an organizational change that reshapes processes, services, culture and relations with stakeholders. Evidence from the OECD likewise shows that digital technologies and data can improve how governments respond and deliver services, but that implementation, evaluation, skills and governance remain challenges. The study concludes that digital transformation can improve the performance of the political system, provided that technological innovation is complemented by institutional reform, inclusive access, transparency, data protection, cybersecurity, human control and effective governance arrangements. Digital transformation should therefore be understood as a governance transformation in which technological capabilities are combined with institutional, legal, organizational and societal factors.

title: When the Metric Cannot See the Model: Structural Decoupling in Simulation-Based Evaluation of Blockchain–AI Supply Chain Systems
summary: Integrated blockchain and machine-learning systems for pharmaceutical supply chains are usually evaluated in simulation, and the headline result is typically a system-level detection rate reported beside the accuracies of the underlying models. This article examines whether such a metric actually responds to those models, using a twelve-node Hyperledger Fabric system with three analytic agents as a controlled test case. A one-factor-at-a-time ablation over three model improvements moved the reported counterfeit detection rate by exactly zero percentage points, because the metric was computed from severity-linked proxy signals rather than from model inference. We state a condition that detects this structural decoupling without running an experiment, show that recalibrating the composite score cannot repair it, and report a pre-registered redesign that replaces the proxies with live inference and with provenance derived from realized custody chains. The redesign restores coupling: degrading the classifier lowers system-level detection from 92.3% to 87.5%, with the same sign on all ten seeds. It also shows that blockchain provenance helps only when counterfeiting is concentrated at identifiable sources, that trust weights calibrated on proxies do not transfer, and that the corrected metric has its own blind spot: a 12.3% false-positive rate that five pre-registered repairs, each confirmed on held-out seeds, failed to reduce at the operating point. The protocol, code, per-seed records, and withdrawn conclusions are released, and a four-question checklist is derived for evaluators of such systems. Preprint, not peer reviewed. title: Bridging leadership competency gaps across different management levels to enable digital transformation in the construction industry
summary: Purpose As the construction industry undergoes digital transformation, the need for adaptive and effective leadership has become increasingly essential. This study aims to investigate the perceived importance and self-assessed performance of leadership competencies across four management levels in the construction industry. Design/methodology/approach Using survey data collected from 305 construction professionals, 25 leadership competencies were evaluated across four management levels: general staff, line management, middle management and senior management. A refined importance-performance analysis (IPA) approach was applied to identify competency gaps and reveal level-specific leadership patterns. Findings The results show distinct competency gap among different management levels. General staff face significant shortfalls in communication and strategic awareness; line managers underperform in coordination, policy implementation and financial management; middle managers struggle with innovation tolerance and interpreting digital strategies; while senior managers exhibit gaps in digital literacy, team motivation, and market research and evaluation. Originality/value Theoretically, the study contributes to digital transformation research in construction by highlighting the differentiated and multi-level nature of leadership under digital transformation. The findings emphasise leadership development in construction as a dynamic process rather than a static leadership style or set of capabilities. Practically, the study proposes a Multi-level Competency Enablement Pathway to guide leadership development strategies tailored to the specific demands of each management level. The findings provide actionable insights for construction organisations seeking to align leadership capability development with the requirements of digital transformation and enhance organisational digital readiness.

title: Risk-aware hierarchical reinforcement learning for investment and operations in cross-border energy supply chains under the belt and road initiative
summary: Abstract Cross-border energy supply chains under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) face unprecedented challenges, including geopolitical instability, macroeconomic volatility, and operational disruptions. Traditional optimization or flat reinforcement learning (RL) methods often struggle to address the scale, uncertainty, and multi-stakeholder complexity inherent in such environments. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a novel hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) framework that separates strategic investment planning from tactical operational control via a two-level architecture. The high-level agent makes long-horizon decisions on resource allocation and infrastructure deployment, while the low-level agent handles real-time logistics under dynamically imposed constraints. The framework explicitly incorporates multi-dimensional risk—political, economic, and operational—into both reward shaping and policy learning. Through extensive simulations on representative BRI corridors, the proposed HRL model demonstrates superior simulated performance over single-level RL, mixed-integer programming, and rule-based baselines across key metrics, including cumulative profit (+ 25%), service-level reliability, and robustness to stress scenarios. Ablation and continual learning experiments further confirm the contributions of hierarchical abstraction and risk-aware training. This work contributes a scalable, interpretable, and risk-resilient decision-making architecture for intelligent energy infrastructure planning in global contexts.

title: Fintech Development and the Net‐Zero Transition: Implications for Environmental Sustainability in Türkiye
summary: ABSTRACT Türkiye plays a significant role in addressing global climate change through its economic, industrial, environmental, and energy policies. As an emerging economy, Türkiye has committed to reducing emissions by 2038 and achieving a net‐zero emission target by 2053. In this context, this study aims to provide additional policy tools to enhance environmental sustainability and reach the net‐zero target. The study examines the linkage among fintech development, energy use, economic growth, and greenhouse gas emissions for the period from 2006q1 to 2024q4. By incorporating Fourier trigonometric terms, we utilize the Fourier ADL approach for the cointegration test and the FMOLS method for long‐term coefficient estimators. The findings indicate that economic growth and energy consumption trigger greenhouse gas emissions in Türkiye. However, the impact of financial development is insignificant. Building on this finding, the study further explores the mechanisms through financial innovation in Türkiye.

title: Persistent Stock Discrepancies In Hospital Pharmacy Supply Chains: Why Robotics, System Integration, And Artificial Intelligence Have Not Closed The Reconciliation Gap
summary: Background: Hospital pharmacies have invested heavily in robotic dispensing, automated storage and retrieval systems (ASRS), automated dispensing cabinets (ADCs), enterprise resource planning (ERP) integration, and, increasingly, artificial intelligence (AI)-based demand forecasting and anomaly detection. Despite this, perpetual-inventory-to-physical-stock discrepancies continue to be reported across acute-care settings. Objective: This paper synthesizes evidence on the causes of residual stock discrepancy in automated and AI-augmented hospital pharmacy supply chains, and proposes a reconciliation framework that treats discrepancy as a systems-integration problem rather than a technology-adoption problem. Methods: A narrative review of peer-reviewed literature, health-system white papers, and vendor-reported case studies on pharmacy automation, radio-frequency identification (RFID), barcode workflows, and AI-enabled inventory analytics was conducted, supplemented by root-cause analysis using a socio-technical systems lens. Findings: Discrepancies persist for five interacting reasons: (1) physical–digital reconciliation gaps at the point of human handling (borrowing, waste, returns, and multi-step dispensing that automation does not fully observe); (2) line-of-sight and data-capture limits of barcode and even some RFID deployments; (3) data latency and fragmentation across ADC, ERP, electronic health record (EHR), and wholesaler systems that are “integrated” at the interface level but not at the transaction level; (4) AI forecasting and anomaly-detection models that are only as reliable as the transactional data they are trained on, and which can mask rather than resolve upstream data-quality defects; and (5) governance and process gaps, including inconsistent downtime procedures, override cultures, and unclear accountability for reconciliation. Case evidence from automated dispensing evaluations and RFID deployments shows measurable improvement in accuracy and time-to-restock, but not elimination of discrepancy. Conclusion: Technology adoption narrows but does not close the reconciliation gap. Sustained reduction in stock discrepancy requires pairing automation and AI with transaction-level data governance, closed-loop verification at every physical handoff, and explicit ownership of exception handling.

title: A Conceptual Study on Eco-Entrepreneurship
summary: Introduction: Sustainability in terms of the environment is the most crucial element for the economic system to function successfully. No matter how much the community has evolved or how much money can be earned from it, everyone's ultimate desire is to live a happy and tranquil life. The use of hazardous materials in combination with hazardous chemicals has skyrocketed in recent years, endangering people's lives. A partial answer to these problems is ecopreneurship, a new branch of entrepreneurship that seeks to create a sustainable way of life on Earth with a healthy atmosphere and better giving to the people. Methodology: The method applied is a qualitative method, comprehensive literature review, secondary information collection and contextualization of the interlinkages, analysing how government supports ecopreneurs by providing technological advancements to develop the Indian economy. The study is organised around three objectives: to analyze the ecopreneurship impact on the Indian economy, to provide technological information to ecopreneurs, and to facilitate government support for ecopreneurs. The literature reviewed includes Schaltegger (2002) on ecopreneurs as creators of business models contributing to environmental sustainability, Alvord, Brown and Letts (2004) on social entrepreneurship, Robert Isaak (2005) on the making of the ecopreneur, Dixon and Clifford (2007) on ecopreneurialstrategies, Huang, Ding and Kao (2009) on green innovations, and Global Urban Development (2010) on green products and services. Results & Discussion: Ecopreneurship combines the words eco, meaning environment, and preneurship, meaning entrepreneurship, and ecopreneurs are those interested in solving environmental issues while taking the environment's long-term health into account. Seven aspects of its significance are identified: environmental conservation, innovation for sustainability, social responsibility, financial prospects, climate change mitigation, support from governments and politicians, and effects on education and public awareness. Ten forces propel ecopreneurship, including environmental awareness, customer demand, regulatory pressures, innovative technologies, global sustainability goals such as the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, corporate social responsibility, efficiency and cost savings, funding access, evolving business culture, and social and ethical values. Ten successful Indian ecopreneurs are documented, among them Manoj Bhargava (Billions in Change), Ankit Agarwal and Karan Rastogi (Help Us Green), Upendra Tripathy (Saur Energy International), Swati Pandey (Aranyaani), R. Gopinath (Agni Solar Systems), Anirudh Sharma (Graviky Labs) and Rajeev Kher (Sustainable Green Initiative). Twelve challenges are identified, including expensive initial costs, financial constraints, market acceptance, absent infrastructure, policy and regulatory barriers, supply chain difficulties, technological risks and difficulties in scaling. Conclusion: A large number of academics have already examined the concept of ecopreneurship, along with its opportunities and difficulties, though most researchers only conducted study in particular geographic regions. The amount of research on this subject is expected to increase as more individuals become conscious of the possible environmental harm that their enterprises may do. It is recommended that people keep up their proactive efforts to save the environment by supporting policies and programs from the government, delivering subsidies and alluring incentives to eco-friendly business owners. The rationale for Indian business owners' adoption of green practices and the role of business consultants in suggesting green initiatives for start-up enterprises are proposed for further investigation.

title: Data-Driven Cybersecurity Risk Assessment in FinTech: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Breach Patterns, Vulnerability Factors and Financial Impact, 2008-2025
summary: As FinTech has grown, digital financial platforms have become major targets for cybercriminals, yet most research on FinTech cybersecurity only describes incidents without measuring patterns or risk. In this study, I built a dataset of 47 publicly reported FinTech cyber incidents from 2008 to 2025, recording the type of company, attack method, records exposed, financial loss and root causes of each, and analysed it using statistical tests and a content analysis of incident narratives. Three clear patterns emerged. First, damage is highly uneven, with just three incidents accounting for almost 70% of the 1.69 billion records exposed. Second, attacks increasingly come through outside vendors and partners. Third-party involvement rose from zero incidents before 2020 to half of all incidents in 2023?2025, and ransomware caused six of the sixteen most recent cases. Third, crypto and DeFi platforms suffered far larger losses, with a median loss of US$290 million compared with US$26 million for other FinTech firms. My findings suggest that FinTech cyber risk now spreads through vendors and shared systems across the ecosystem rather than through attacks on single companies. Based on this, I propose a five-stage framework that FinTech firms can use to assess and prioritise their cyber risks.

title: EPISTEMIC RESISTANCE: Local Knowledge, Autonomous Governance, and the Politics of Co-optation
summary: Global environmental governance is overwhelmingly dictated by Western technocratic rationality, systematically marginalizing Indigenous and Local Knowledge (ILK) through structural epistemic violence. This study critically investigates how market-based climate regimes, voluntary carbon offset mechanisms, and state land formalization programs co-opt and transform localized, relational ecological knowledge into commodified instruments of green extraction. Following the PRISMA 2020 protocol, a systematic literature review was conducted across Scopus, Web of Science, and JSTOR (2005–2026), yielding a synthesis corpus of 110 peer-reviewed studies spanning Critical Political Ecology, Decolonial Philosophy, and Feminist Political Ecology. Findings reveal a structural paradox: shallow inclusion and carbon commodification via frameworks such as REDD+ sever ILK from its socio-spiritual contexts and territorial sovereignty, transforming customary stewards into administrative compliance officers. Conversely, subaltern communities actively operationalize epistemic resistance through digital counter-mapping, epistemic disobedience, the revitalization of customary legal governance (e.g., Tara-Bandu, Sasi), and multi-scalar solidarity networks. The study concludes that physical land reclamation is fundamentally insufficient without the concurrent reclamation of epistemic sovereignty. To bridge this critical governance gap, we propose an embodied eco-social contract that re-anchors global environmental governance in epistemological pluralism, direct climate finance decentralization, and substantive legal recognition of sovereign living territories (territorios de vida). Keywords: Epistemic Violence; Epistemic Resistance; Indigenous and Local Knowledge (ILK); Green Grabbing; Counter-Mapping; Autonomous Governance; Political Ecology.

title: Implementation Gaps in Sharia Audit for Strengthening Islamic Financial Governance in Indonesia
summary: This study aims to examine the sharia audit within the framework of Islamic financial governance and to identify existing implementation gaps in Indonesia through a literature review approach. The findings reveal that sharia audit serves a strategic role as an assurance mechanism, ensuring alignment between sharia principles and the operational practices of Islamic financial institutions. Nevertheless, its implementation remains constrained by several challenges, including the absence of fully integrated sharia audit standards, a shortage of qualified human resources, and the limited integration of audit functions within broader governance systems. Furthermore, variations in interpretation and institutional capacity contribute to inconsistencies in audit practices across institutions. Although international standards issued by the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) provide an important normative benchmark, their adoption within the Indonesian context remains suboptimal. Accordingly, strengthening sharia audit practices requires a comprehensive and systemic approach, encompassing regulatory harmonization, capacity building for human resources, and the development of more practical and applicable audit methodologies.

title: Ethical Bias in AI Datasets: A Data Science Audit Framework for Fairness and Transparency (DS-Audit v1.0)
summary: As AI systems are increasingly deployed in hiring, finance, and governance, ethical bias embedded in training datasets poses a critical risk to fairness and transparency. This technical report presents DS-Audit v1.0, a five-phase Data Science Audit Framework for systematic evaluation and mitigation of dataset bias. The framework is designed for independent researchers, startups, and academic institutions to perform responsible AI auditing without enterprise infrastructure. A case study in the Indian IT hiring context demonstrates practical applicability, where Disparate Impact improved from 0.41 to 0.88 after mitigation.

title: Pengaruh Audit Tenure dan Audit Kinerja Terhadap Kualitas Audit Pada Perusahaan Sub Sektor Minyak, Gas, dan Batu Bara yang Terdaftar di Bursa Efek Indonesia Periode 2023–2025
summary: ABSTRACT This study aims to examine and analyze the effect of audit tenure and audit performance on audit quality in oil, gas, and coal sub-sector companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) during the 2023–2025 period. The extractive sector was chosen because of its high accounting complexity, involving reserve estimation, impairment of exploration assets, environmental restoration obligations, and commodity price volatility, all of which place heavy demands on audit quality. This research employs a quantitative descriptive-verificative approach using secondary data obtained from the annual reports of sample companies published on www.idx.co.id. The population consists of 89 listed companies, and through purposive sampling, 23 companies were selected as the research sample, observed over three years (2023–2025), producing 69 firm-year observations that were reduced to 44 observations after outlier treatment to satisfy the classical assumption of normality. Audit tenure is measured by the length of consecutive audit engagement, audit performance is proxied by the natural logarithm of audit fees, and audit quality is measured using discretionary accruals based on the Modified Jones Model. Data were analyzed using multiple linear regression with the aid of SPSS version 26. The results show that audit tenure has a significant negative effect on audit quality, audit performance has a significant positive effect on audit quality, and both variables simultaneously have a significant effect on audit quality, with an adjusted R square of 23.8 percent. These findings support agency theory, in which the duration of the audit engagement and the depth of audit resource allocation jointly determine the auditor's capacity to reduce information asymmetry between principals and agents in the extractive industry. Keywords: Audit Tenure, Audit Performance, Audit Quality, Extractive Industry. ABSTRAK Studi ini dilakukan untuk mengidentifikasi serta membuktikan dampak masa jabatan auditor (audit tenure) dan audit kinerja terhadap tingkat kualitas audit yang dihasilkan pada perusahaan subsektor minyak, gas, serta batubara yang tercatat di Bursa Efek Indonesia sepanjang 2023–2025. title: Does CEO AI literacy curb ESG greenwashing? Evidence from China
summary: This study examines whether CEO AI literacy curbs or amplifies ESG greenwashing. Using 10,820 firm-year observations of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2019 to 2022, we construct CEO AI literacy from resume-based evidence of AI-related education, work experience, and executive background. We find that CEO AI literacy significantly reduces ESG greenwashing, suggesting that technological cognition promotes substantive ESG practices rather than symbolic disclosure. This effect is stronger in high-tech industries, where digital infrastructure enables CEOs’ AI capabilities to translate more effectively into ESG monitoring and transparency. The findings remain robust to PSM and entropy balancing. This study contributes by identifying CEO-level AI literacy as a micro-foundation of ESG authenticity.

title: The Effect of Fintech Payment Development on Firm Value in the Indonesian Banking Sector with Profitability as a Mediating Variable
summary: This study examines fintech payment development (FBIR) and firm value (PBV), with profitability (ROA) as a mediator and firm size as a control. Data comprise 125 observations from 25 Indonesian listed conventional banks in KBMI groups 2–4 during 2020–2024. Fixed effects panel regression and the Sobel test reveal no statistically significant effects of FBIR on ROA or PBV, or of ROA on PBV. Profitability does not significantly mediate the relationship. Firm size positively and significantly affects ROA. Robustness checks support these findings, indicating insufficient evidence linking fintech payment development to profitability and market valuation within the sample. title: Review Protocol — Intellectual Capital and Market Performance: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: This document is the protocol for a systematic literature review of the relationship between intellectual capital (IC) and market-based firm performance. It was deposited before the final literature search to fix the research questions, eligibility criteria, search strategy, and analysis plan in advance. The review addresses four research questions: (1) the development and structure of research on IC and market performance; (2) the theories, methods, IC and market performance proxies, and contexts used; (3) why empirical findings diverge across IC components and proxies, market performance measures, countries, sectors, and methods; and (4) the extent to which ESG, earnings quality, and corporate governance have been examined as mediators or moderators. Scopus is the main database, supplemented by Google Scholar and citation chasing. Eligible studies are English-language journal articles up to 2025 that use archival firm-level data and test IC as an independent variable against at least one market-based performance measure (e.g., Tobin's Q, market-to-book ratio, stock return). The review combines bibliometric analysis (VOSviewer) with content synthesis, tests five competing explanations for divergent findings, and reports gaps as counts; a meta-analysis of partial correlations is planned if data allow. Reporting follows PRISMA 2020. AI tools (Elicit, NotebookLM) assist screening and are verified by the author.
